intro: The Bible opens with God creating "the heavens and the earth" (Genesis 1:1). It closes with "a new heaven and a new earth" (Revelation 21:1). Between these two texts, the phrase appears again and again. Sometimes it plainly means the sky and the ground. At other times it seems to carry a second meaning. Moses calls heaven and earth as witnesses against Israel. Isaiah says God planted the heavens when he said to Zion, "You are my people." Jeremiah sees the land of Judah return to "formless and empty". Jesus says heaven and earth will pass away, in the same breath as a promise about "this generation". This study asks one main question: when Scripture speaks of heaven and earth passing away and being made new, does it mean the physical universe, the covenant world of Israel centred on the temple, or both? It sets out the covenantal (fulfilled) reading at its strongest. This reading holds that the old-covenant order, with its temple, priests and sacrifices, was a small "heaven and earth" that passed away in AD 70, and that the new heavens and new earth are the new-covenant world in Christ. It also gives the other main readings fairly: the renewal of this creation, its dissolution and replacement, the already/not-yet view, and the full preterist and covenant-creation positions. Along the way it looks at the tabernacle as a small model of the cosmos (Josephus, Antiquities 3.7.7; Jewish War 5.5.4-5), creation words that return when God forms, judges or renews his people, key Hebrew and Greek words, and Isaiah 65-66 beside Revelation 21-22. Every view here is held by Christians who love Scripture. The aim is to understand each one well, not to win an argument.

views.name: Renewal of this creation
views.summary: God will not throw away the world he made. At Christ's return he will free it from decay and make it new, the way he will raise our bodies. The new earth is this earth, healed and glorified.
views.keyClaim: The new heavens and new earth are this same cosmos renewed, set free from the curse at the resurrection of the body.
views.holders: Irenaeus; John Calvin; Abraham Kuyper; Herman Bavinck; Anthony Hoekema; Albert Wolters; N. T. Wright; J. Richard Middleton; many Reformed, Catholic and Orthodox teachers.
views.strengths: It fits Romans 8, where creation itself waits to be freed, and Acts 3:21, which speaks of the restoring of all things. It keeps a close link between the resurrection of the body and the renewal of the world: Jesus' body was the same body, changed. It honours God's verdict that creation is good (Genesis 1:31). Early manuscripts of 2 Peter 3:10 read "will be found" or "laid bare", which suggests purging, not erasing.
views.weaknesses: Texts such as 2 Peter 3:10-12, Isaiah 51:6 and Revelation 20:11 use strong language of passing, melting and fleeing, which a renewal reading must soften. It usually treats Matthew 24:35 as a proverb about the stability of Jesus' words, which some find weak beside verse 34. Covenantal readers say it overlooks how often "heaven and earth" language is used for Israel's covenant order.

views.name: Dissolution and replacement
views.summary: The present universe will be burned up and pass out of existence. God will then create a brand-new heaven and earth. 2 Peter 3:10 is read literally: the elements are the physical building blocks of matter.
views.keyClaim: The physical heavens and earth will be destroyed by fire, and God will create a wholly new universe in their place.
views.holders: Lutheran orthodoxy (Johann Gerhard; later Francis Pieper) spoke of the annihilation of the world's substance; many dispensational writers such as John Walvoord and J. Dwight Pentecost; many popular Bible teachers.
views.strengths: It takes the strong words of 2 Peter 3 and Revelation 20:11 ("earth and heaven fled away") at face value. Psalms 102:25-26 and Hebrews 1:10-12 contrast the perishing creation with the unchanging Lord. It stresses that the new world is God's gift, not a human achievement.
views.weaknesses: It sits uneasily with Romans 8:21, where creation itself is set free, not destroyed. The flood comparison in 2 Peter 3:6 involves a world that "perished" yet was not annihilated. The best manuscripts of 2 Peter 3:10 end with "will be found", not "burned up". It also struggles with texts that say the earth stands for ever (Psalms 104:5; Ecclesiastes 1:4).

views.name: Covenantal reading of the passing texts, with a future resurrection
views.summary: Several "passing" texts describe the end of the old-covenant order in AD 70. This includes Matthew 24:35, Hebrews 12:26-28 and, for some, 2 Peter 3 and Revelation 21. But Christ's bodily return, the resurrection of the dead and the final judgment are still future.
views.keyClaim: "Heaven and earth" in key prophecies is covenant language for the temple-centred world of Israel, which passed in AD 70; the final resurrection is still to come.
views.holders: Some partial preterists. John Lightfoot (1602-1675) read Matthew 24:29-35 of Jerusalem's fall. John Owen (1616-1683) read 2 Peter 3:5-13 and Hebrews 12:26-27 as including the end of the Jewish church-state. John Brown of Edinburgh read Matthew 5:18 this way. Modern writers such as James Jordan and Peter Leithart. Others in this camp, such as J. Marcellus Kik and Kenneth Gentry, read Matthew 24:35 or 2 Peter 3 of the final end.
views.strengths: It takes the time words seriously: "this generation" (Matthew 24:34), "ready to vanish" (Hebrews 8:13), "yet once more" (Hebrews 12:26). It uses the prophets' own language of cosmic collapse for the fall of nations (Isaiah 13:10; Ezekiel 32:7). It has respected older Protestant voices. It keeps the creeds' future hope.
views.weaknesses: Critics say it can blur when a text means the old covenant and when it means the cosmos, and partial preterists disagree among themselves about which texts belong where. Revelation 21:4 promises no more death, which seems beyond AD 70. Some argue that 2 Peter 3:5-7 compares the coming fire with a real flood on the physical world.

views.name: Full preterist covenant-world reading
views.summary: All end-time prophecy, including the coming of Christ, the resurrection and the new heavens and new earth, was fulfilled in the events that closed with AD 70. The new Jerusalem of Revelation 21 is the church in the new covenant now.
views.keyClaim: The first heaven and earth of Revelation 21:1 is the old-covenant world; it passed in AD 70, and the new creation is the present new-covenant age in its fullness.
views.holders: J. Stuart Russell (The Parousia, 1878) is often seen as the classic statement; Max R. King; Don K. Preston; others in the modern preterist movement.
views.strengths: It is very consistent with the time texts of Revelation ("soon", "near", Revelation 1:1, 3; 22:10). It reads Revelation 21 in line with Isaiah 65, where death and sinners still exist (Isaiah 65:20). It explains why the bride, the city and the holy mountain are pictures of a people (Revelation 21:9-10).
views.weaknesses: It sets aside the future bodily resurrection and final judgment that all the historic creeds confess. Most Christians, including most partial preterists, see it as outside historic orthodoxy. Critics point to 1 Corinthians 15:42-54, 1 Thessalonians 4:16-17 and the warning against those who said the resurrection had already happened (2 Timothy 2:18). The ongoing reality of death seems hard to square with Revelation 21:4.

views.name: Covenant-creation reading of Genesis 1
views.summary: This reading goes further. It says Genesis 1 itself is not mainly about the making of the physical universe. It describes God forming his covenant people, the first "heavens and earth" that later passed away. This is a minority view even among full preterists, and many of them reject it.
views.keyClaim: The "heavens and earth" of Genesis 1:1 are the covenant world God began with Adam, so the passing of the "first heaven and earth" (Revelation 21:1) completes the story that Genesis 1 began.
views.holders: A small group within full preterism, set out at length by Timothy Martin and Jeffrey Vaughn (Beyond Creation Science, 2007). Most preterists, partial and full, do not hold it. Almost no other Christian tradition does.
views.strengths: It notices real links: Jeremiah 4:23 uses Genesis 1:2 words for Judah's ruin, and Isaiah 51:16 uses creation words for Israel's founding. It reads the Bible as one covenant story from first page to last. Its defenders say it frees Genesis from being forced into modern science debates.
views.weaknesses: Genesis 1 names plants, sea creatures, birds, cattle and the lights in the sky, which read as the physical world. Other texts look back to Genesis 1 as the making of all things: Exodus 20:11, Psalms 104, Acts 14:15, Romans 1:20, and Jesus in Mark 10:6. Key word arguments (such as "host" in Genesis 2:1 meaning a mass of people) are not supported by most Hebrew scholars. It cuts the covenant from the created world rather than placing it within it.

views.name: Inaugurated new creation: already and not yet
views.summary: The new creation has already begun in the risen Christ and in all who are joined to him. Yet the full renewal of the cosmos waits for his return. The old-covenant order ended with the cross and AD 70, but the new heavens and earth will be complete only at the resurrection.
views.keyClaim: New creation is present now in Christ and his people, and will be completed in a renewed cosmos at his coming.
views.holders: G. K. Beale (A New Testament Biblical Theology, 2011); Geerhardus Vos; Herman Ridderbos; Anthony Hoekema; Douglas Moo; many amillennial and postmillennial teachers.
views.strengths: It explains why Paul can say the new creation is here (2 Corinthians 5:17) while creation still groans (Romans 8:22). It matches the pattern of Christ's resurrection as the "firstfruits" of a later harvest (1 Corinthians 15:23). It can accept much of the covenantal reading of the temple while keeping the cosmic hope.
views.weaknesses: Preterist readers say it delays texts that carry near time words. Some replacement readers say it makes the new earth too much like the present one. Its users do not always agree where a given text sits on the "already" or "not yet" side.

groups.title: What did Jesus mean by "heaven and earth will pass away"?
groups.summary: Matthew 24:34-35 and its parallels set a time limit and speak of heaven and earth passing. These questions ask whether Jesus meant the cosmos, the temple order, or simply that his words outlast all things.

groups.title: Was the temple a small heaven and earth?
groups.summary: Josephus and later readers saw the tabernacle and temple as a model of the cosmos. These questions look at that idea and what it means when the temple falls.

groups.title: Can "heaven and earth" stand for a people?
groups.summary: Moses speaks to the heavens and earth as witnesses. Abraham's seed is like the stars and the dust. Joseph's dream uses sun, moon and stars for a family. These questions test how far this picture language goes.

groups.title: How do the Psalms use heaven and earth?
groups.summary: The Psalms call the heavens to praise, to declare, to witness and to perish like a garment. These questions ask when the words mean sky and ground and when they point to God's people.

groups.title: Why do the prophets shake the heavens?
groups.summary: Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Joel and Haggai use darkened suns and shaken heavens for judgment on nations and on Israel. These questions look at that language and its use in the New Testament.

groups.title: What passes away in 2 Peter 3 and Revelation 21?
groups.summary: 2 Peter 3 speaks of fire and melting elements; Revelation 21 of a first heaven and earth that passed away. These questions weigh the covenantal and the cosmic readings.

groups.title: What are the new heavens and the new earth?
groups.summary: Isaiah 65-66 and Revelation 21-22 describe a new world, a new Jerusalem and a people of joy. These questions ask whether this is the church now, the renewed cosmos later, or both.

groups.title: How should we decide, and why does it matter?
groups.summary: These questions deal with method: Scripture and tradition, the creeds, literal and figurative reading, and what difference each view makes for faith and life.

questions.q: Did Jesus mean that the physical universe would vanish within one generation?
questions.short: On the fulfilled reading, no. Jesus tied the passing of "heaven and earth" to his own generation, so he must have meant the old covenant world centred on the temple, not the stars and the planet.
questions.answer: In Matthew 24:34-35 Jesus says two things side by side. First, "this generation" will not pass until all these things happen. Second, heaven and earth will pass, but his words will not. If "heaven and earth" meant the physical cosmos, the prophecy failed, because the sky and the ground are still here. Read covenantally, the saying fits its setting. Jesus had just left the temple and said that not one stone would stay on another (Matthew 24:1-2). The disciples asked when this would happen. The answer ends with a pledge: the old order will go, but my word stands. In AD 70 the temple, the priesthood and the sacrifices ended. On this reading, that was the "heaven and earth" that passed, and it passed inside the forty years Jesus gave.
examples: Jesus spoke about AD 30. The temple burned in August AD 70 (Josephus, Jewish War 6.4.5-8), about forty years later, the length of one biblical generation.
Mark 13:30-31 and Luke 21:32-33 repeat the same two sayings together, so the link between "this generation" and "heaven and earth" is in all three Gospels.
questions.other: Many futurists and amillennialists say verse 35 is a proverb: even if the universe passed away, Christ's words would not. Others, including some partial preterists, see verse 35 as a turn toward the final end of the present cosmos at the second coming, with verse 34 limited to AD 70.

questions.q: Does Scripture say the earth will remain forever?
questions.short: Yes. Several texts say God founded the earth so that it stands forever. The fulfilled reading uses this to argue that the "heaven and earth" which passes away must be something other than the physical planet.
questions.answer: Psalms 104:5 says God set the earth on its foundations so that it will never be moved. Ecclesiastes 1:4 says generations come and go, but the earth stays forever. Psalms 78:69 says God built his sanctuary like the high heavens, like the earth he founded forever. On the fulfilled reading, Scripture does not contradict itself. If the physical earth abides, then texts about heaven and earth "passing away" must use the phrase in a covenant sense. Psalms 78:69 even compares the temple to heaven and earth. That supports the idea that the temple world could be called "heaven and earth". When that sanctuary fell, a covenant "heaven and earth" ended, while the physical earth went on.
examples: Psalms 78:69 likens the Jerusalem sanctuary to the heights and to the earth. The temple was built to mirror the cosmos.
Ecclesiastes 1:4 contrasts passing human generations with the earth that stays. The point is the earth's lasting, not its end.
questions.other: Other readers note that the Hebrew word olam can mean "for a very long age" rather than "without end". They say these texts praise the earth's stability under God, and do not rule out a final renewal of creation (Romans 8:21; 2 Peter 3:13). Many hold that the earth is renewed, not destroyed, so it still "remains".

questions.q: If the physical cosmos did not pass away, what "heaven and earth" did pass away in that generation?
questions.short: On the covenantal reading, it was the old covenant order: the temple, its priesthood and sacrifices, and the nation built around them. That world ended when Rome destroyed Jerusalem in AD 70.
questions.answer: Jesus spoke these words while predicting the fall of the temple (Matthew 24:1-2). The prophets often used "heaven and earth" for a people and its ruling order. Isaiah spoke of God planting the heavens and founding the earth when he said to Zion, "You are my people" (Isaiah 51:16). Jeremiah described Judah's ruin as the earth returning to "formless and empty" (Jeremiah 4:23). Hebrews, written while the temple still stood, said the first covenant was old and "ready to vanish away" (Hebrews 8:13). On the fulfilled reading, these lines meet in AD 70. The temple, the centre of Israel's world, was burned. Sacrifice stopped. The old covenant structure passed, and the new covenant order in Christ stood alone.
examples: Hebrews 8:13: the first covenant was "growing old" and near to vanishing. The writer spoke as if the end was close.
Josephus reports that the temple was burned on the same day of the year that Babylon had burned the first temple (Jewish War 6.4.5).
questions.other: Futurists and most amillennialists answer that no "heaven and earth" has yet passed; Jesus was speaking of the final end. Partial preterists who divide the chapter say AD 70 fulfilled verses 1-34, but verse 35 looks to the end of the present cosmos. All agree AD 70 ended the temple system.

questions.q: Did the disciples ask about the end of the world or the end of the age (Matthew 24:3)?
questions.short: They asked about the end of the "age" (Greek aion), after Jesus foretold the temple's fall. The fulfilled reading says they meant the end of the old covenant age, not the end of the physical world.
questions.answer: Jesus had just said that Jerusalem's house would be left desolate (Matthew 23:38) and that the temple stones would be thrown down (24:2). The disciples asked three things: when this will happen, what sign will show his coming, and what will mark the end of the age (24:3). The Greek word is aion, "age", not kosmos, "world". Older English Bibles said "end of the world", which led many readers to think of the planet. On the fulfilled reading, a Jew in AD 30 linked the fall of the temple with the close of an era. Jesus did not correct their question. He answered it, and placed it within "this generation" (24:34).
examples: The KJV says "end of the world"; most modern versions say "end of the age", which follows the Greek aion.
Hebrews 9:26 uses the same phrase in the plural: Christ appeared "at the end of the ages" to put away sin. That was in the first century.
questions.other: Futurist and many amillennial readers agree the word is "age", but they say "this age" runs until Christ's return (Matthew 13:39-40; 28:20). They hold that the disciples blended the temple's fall with the final end, and Jesus answered both, which is why his reply looks near and far.

questions.q: What do "the end of the age" and "the age to come" mean?
questions.short: On the fulfilled reading, "this age" was the age of the Mosaic covenant and "the age to come" was the messianic age of the new covenant. The changeover came between the cross and AD 70.
questions.answer: Paul told the Corinthians that "the ends of the ages" had come upon them (1 Corinthians 10:11). Hebrews says Christ appeared "at the end of the ages" (Hebrews 9:26). Peter called his own time "these last times" (1 Peter 1:20) and said "the end of all things is at hand" (1 Peter 4:7). Jewish teachers spoke of "this age" and "the age to come", meaning the time before and after the Messiah. Jesus used the same pair in Matthew 12:32. On the fulfilled reading, the old age closed when the temple and its sacrifices ended. The age to come is the Christian era, where the blood of Christ cleanses the conscience (Hebrews 9:14). Older scholars such as Milton Terry read Matthew 24:3 in this way.
examples: 1 Corinthians 10:11, written about AD 55, says the ends of the ages had reached Paul's readers.
Matthew 12:32 speaks of forgiveness "neither in this age nor in the age to come", the common Jewish two-age pattern.
questions.other: Many scholars, including amillennialists and dispensationalists, hold that the "age to come" fully begins at Christ's return and the resurrection (Luke 20:34-36). They speak of an "already and not yet": the new age broke in with Christ, but the present evil age continues until the end (Galatians 1:4).

questions.q: Does Jesus change the subject at Matthew 24:35-36?
questions.short: The fulfilled reading in this chapter says no. Verse 35 sums up the darkened sun and falling stars of verse 29, and verse 36 speaks of the exact day of that same judgment, which only the Father knew.
questions.answer: Some respected partial preterists, such as J. Marcellus Kik and Kenneth Gentry, hold that verses 1-34 describe AD 70 and that verse 36 moves to the final coming. Charles Spurgeon also saw a change at verse 36. The fulfilled reading in this chapter disagrees. Verse 35 does not start a new topic. It confirms what Jesus has just said. Verse 29 used the old prophetic picture of a falling sky. Verse 35 says the same thing in plain words: heaven and earth will pass. Verse 36 then adds that the day and hour are unknown. The disciples had asked "when" (24:3). Jesus gave the generation (24:34), but not the day. John Gill and John Lightfoot both read verse 36 as the day of Jerusalem's fall.
examples: Jesus told them to pray that their flight would not be in winter or on a Sabbath (Matthew 24:20). This shows that the exact season was unknown even inside the generation.
Adam Clarke noted that the Greek hora can mean "season" and tied verse 36 to the siege of Jerusalem.
questions.other: Those who see a change point to "but of that day" (Greek peri de), which often marks a new topic (1 Corinthians 7:1). They note that signs are given before verse 34 but none after, and that the later parables stress delay. They read verses 36-25:46 as the final return.

questions.q: Are the darkened sun and falling stars of Matthew 24:29 another way to say "heaven and earth will pass away"?
questions.short: On the fulfilled reading, yes. The prophets used a collapsing sky to describe the fall of a nation and its rulers. Verse 29 uses that language for Jerusalem, and verse 35 says it again plainly.
questions.answer: Jesus quotes the prophets in verse 29. Isaiah 13:10 used the darkened sun, moon and stars for the fall of Babylon. Isaiah 34:4 used the rolling up of the sky for the judgment of Edom. In Scripture, when stars fall to earth, it pictures rulers brought low (Isaiah 14:12; Daniel 8:10). On the fulfilled reading, Jesus uses the same picture for the end of Israel's ruling order. Verse 29 says it happens "immediately after the tribulation of those days". Verse 34 says it happens in this generation. So the sky falling in verse 29 and heaven and earth passing in verse 35 describe one event: the end of the old covenant world of the temple, upheld by the leaders who "crucified the Lord of glory" (1 Corinthians 2:8).
examples: Babylon fell to the Medes and Persians in 539 BC. The stars did not literally fall, yet Isaiah 13:10 used that picture for it.
Daniel 8:10 shows a horn throwing some stars to the ground. Daniel 8:24 explains them as "the holy people".
questions.other: Most futurists take verse 29 as real cosmic signs before Christ's return (Luke 21:25-26). Many amillennialists see both a near and a final meaning. Even many who accept the prophetic imagery still say verse 35, unlike verse 29, contrasts lasting words with a literally passing cosmos.

questions.q: Does "this generation" (24:34) versus "that day" (24:36) prove that two different events are meant?
questions.short: The fulfilled reading says no. "That" is the natural word for any future point, near or far. "That day" can be the still-future day within "this generation" when Jerusalem would fall.
questions.answer: Some argue that if Jesus meant the same event, he would have said "this day". But "this" points to something present and "that" points to something farther off. The standard Greek lexicon of Arndt and Gingrich notes the same sense for houtos (this) and ekeinos (that). The generation was present when Jesus spoke. The day of judgment was still future, so it was "that day". Prophets often called a coming judgment "that day" when it was near. On the fulfilled reading, "that day" is the day the Son of Man came against Jerusalem, a day still ahead for the disciples, but inside their lifetime.
examples: Isaiah 2:12-20 and Zephaniah 1:7-15 call coming judgments on Judah "that day"; those came on Judah in history.
Luke 17:31 says "in that day" about fleeing from the housetop, a warning tied to the war on Jerusalem.
questions.other: Partial preterists such as Kenneth Gentry argue the shift from "this" to "that" is a deliberate contrast between near and far. Futurists add that Jesus said even he did not know the day, which they think fits a distant final coming better than an event he had just placed within a generation.

questions.q: Why does Jesus give no signs after Matthew 24:36?
questions.short: On the fulfilled reading, the signs had already been given in verses 4-34. After that, Jesus moves from signs to a call for watchfulness, because the exact day would still come by surprise.
questions.answer: Some say that verses 1-34 have many signs, but verses 36-51 have none, so a different, sign-less event must be meant. The fulfilled reading offers two answers. First, all the signs needed to know the general time were already listed: false messiahs, wars, persecution, the gospel preached, and armies around Jerusalem (Luke 21:20). Second, the teaching changes from "what to look for" to "how to live while you wait". A person can know a season and still not know the hour. Jesus says this himself: when you see the fig tree put out leaves, you know summer is near (Matthew 24:32-33). Yet the master still comes at an hour the servant does not expect (24:44).
examples: Luke 21:20-21: when you see Jerusalem surrounded by armies, flee. This was a clear sign. Christians fled to Pella before the siege (Eusebius, Church History 3.5.3).
A farmer knows harvest is near from the crops, but not the day the storm will come.
questions.other: Readers who see two events say the contrast is real: an event with signs (AD 70) and an event with no warning (the final return, 1 Thessalonians 5:2-3). They argue that saying "no one knows the day" right after giving a generation shows the second event has no date limit.

questions.q: Do the plural "those days" and the singular "that day" point to two different events?
questions.short: The fulfilled reading says no. The "days" are the time of tribulation before the end. The "day" is the single day when judgment fell. Both belong to the same generation, as with Noah.
questions.answer: Some argue that the many "days" of the great tribulation (Matthew 24:22) belong to AD 70, but the one "day" (24:36) must be the second coming, which happens in a moment. The fulfilled reading answers that verse 29 says the sky falls "immediately after the tribulation of those days". So the days lead up to a day. Jesus himself uses this pattern with Noah: "the days before the flood" and "the day Noah entered the ark" (24:38). The same people lived through both the days and the day. In the same way, the generation lived through the tribulation and then the day when the city and sanctuary fell.
examples: Noah's neighbours lived through the "days" of warning and then the one "day" the flood came (Genesis 7:11-13).
The siege of Jerusalem lasted months (spring to September AD 70), but the temple burned on a single day (Josephus, Jewish War 6.4.5).
questions.other: Kenneth Gentry and others say the contrast is meaningful: the long tribulation versus a sudden coming "in the twinkling of an eye" (1 Corinthians 15:52). Futurists agree and place the singular day at the end of history.

questions.q: What does "as in the days of Noah" teach: great wickedness or ordinary life?
questions.short: Jesus stresses ordinary life: eating, drinking and marrying. People carried on as usual and did not expect judgment. The point is surprise, not a list of special sins.
questions.answer: Some popular teachers have said "marrying and giving in marriage" means sexual sin or wife-swapping. The text does not say that. Marrying is normal (Matthew 22:30). Luke adds the days of Lot: people bought, sold, planted and built (Luke 17:28). These are everyday tasks. D. A. Carson notes that Jesus makes no direct mention of the sin of that generation here. Noah's age was wicked (Genesis 6:5), but the point of the comparison is that life looked normal. On the fulfilled reading, Jerusalem in the 60s AD was the same. Life went on, and many ignored the warning until the armies came. Peter speaks of mockers who say all things continue as they were (2 Peter 3:3-4).
examples: Noah was warned about "things not yet seen" (Hebrews 11:7). His neighbours saw no sign in the sky.
Luke 17:28-29 lists buying, selling, planting and building in Sodom: daily business, not crimes.
questions.other: Most interpreters of every school agree that the stress is on normal life and surprise. Some dispensational writers add that the end-time world will also be morally corrupt, as in Noah's day, and read Luke's list as showing a careless, godless culture.

questions.q: Are those "taken" in Matthew 24:40-41 taken in a rapture or taken in judgment?
questions.short: In context, they are taken in judgment. The flood "took them all away", and Luke says it "destroyed them all". Noah was the one left to carry on.
questions.answer: Jesus links the two people in the field to the flood: it came and "took them all away" (Matthew 24:39). Luke states the same fact as "destroyed them all" (Luke 17:27, 29). So "taken" means taken by judgment. Noah and his family were the ones left. When the disciples asked "Where, Lord?", Jesus answered that where the body is, the vultures gather (Luke 17:37). That points to death, not rescue. Even the dispensational scholar John Walvoord wrote that in this passage the one taken is taken in judgment. On the fulfilled reading, this fits Judea in AD 66-70, when many were killed or carried off by Roman soldiers, while those who fled survived.
examples: Josephus says about 97,000 were taken captive in the war (Jewish War 6.9.3).
Luke 17:34-37: two in a bed, two grinding, two in a field; then the answer about vultures gathering over a body.
questions.other: Some pretribulation writers, and some posttribulationists such as Robert Gundry, read "taken" as the gathering of believers, since a different Greek verb (paralambano, "take along") is used in 24:40 and in John 14:3. Many others, including Walvoord, agree the one taken is judged.

questions.q: Why does Luke 17 give the same sayings as Matthew 24, but in a different order?
questions.short: Luke places the Noah saying before the housetop, lightning and vulture sayings, which Matthew puts in his AD 70 section. The fulfilled reading says this shows they all speak of the same judgment.
questions.answer: Luke 17:22-37 has five sayings found in Matthew 24: lightning, Noah, the housetop, Lot's wife or "remember", and the vultures. If Matthew's order is 1-2-3-4-5, Luke's is roughly 2-4-1-5-3. Matthew puts the housetop, lightning and vultures before verse 34. Luke puts them together with the Noah saying, which some place after the "turn" at verse 36. On the fulfilled reading, this mixing makes it hard to split Matthew 24 into a near part and a far part. If the Gospel writers could move the sayings freely, then they saw them as one topic. Ray Summers admitted the passage warns against being dogmatic.
examples: Matthew 24:17-18 (housetop) comes before verse 34; in Luke 17:31 it comes after the Noah saying (17:26-27).
Matthew 24:28 (vultures) is before verse 34; in Luke 17:37 it is the last line, after "one taken, one left".
questions.other: Others answer that Luke 17 is a different talk, given on the road (Luke 17:11), and that Luke has his own AD 70 discourse in chapter 21. They say Luke 17 speaks of the final coming, so the order does not settle Matthew's structure. Some critics see the Gospels arranging sayings by theme.

questions.q: Do "a long time" and the bridegroom's "delay" in Matthew 24-25 require a gap of many centuries?
questions.short: The fulfilled reading says no. In each parable the master returns to the same servants, and the bridegroom comes the same night. "A long time" is measured within one lifetime.
questions.answer: The wicked servant says, "My master delays" (Matthew 24:48). Yet the master returns and punishes that same servant (24:50-51). In the parable of the talents, "after a long time" the master settles accounts with the same servants (25:19). In the parable of the virgins, they grow sleepy, and the bridegroom comes at midnight (25:5-6). In each case the delay is real, but short enough for the same people to be there. Elsewhere in the New Testament, "a long time" means months or years, never ages (Luke 23:8; Acts 14:28). On the fulfilled reading, the parables warn a generation that would wait some decades and be tempted to doubt. That matches the mockers of 2 Peter 3:3-4.
examples: Herod "had wanted to see Jesus for a long time" (Luke 23:8). That was a few years at most.
A delay from dusk to midnight is a long wait for a wedding party, but it is still one night.
questions.other: Others, including some partial preterists, say the parables teach delay so that the church will not expect the end too soon. They see the servants as types of the church in every age, so the time scale belongs to the story, not to history. Futurists read the delay as the whole church age.

questions.q: Is the "coming of the Son of Man" in Matthew 24:37 and 25:31 a different coming from the one in 24:27 and 24:30?
questions.short: The fulfilled reading says there is no sign of two comings. Jesus uses the same words for both. He marks "this generation" and "that day", but never "this coming" and "that coming".
questions.answer: Jesus speaks of the coming of the Son of Man in Matthew 24:27, 30, 37, 39 and 44, and in 25:31. If he meant two comings thousands of years apart, the disciples would need some sign of it. None is given. Matthew 25:31 is very close to Matthew 16:27: the Son of Man comes in glory with his angels to repay each person. In the next verse Jesus says some standing there would not die before they saw the Son of Man coming in his kingdom (16:28). On the fulfilled reading, the same coming is in view in all these texts. It is Christ coming in judgment and kingdom power within that generation, as in Daniel 7:13, where the Son of Man comes to the Ancient of Days.
examples: Matthew 16:27-28 and 25:31 share the same parts: Son of Man, glory, angels, judging by deeds.
Daniel 7:13-14: the Son of Man comes on clouds to the Ancient of Days and receives a kingdom.
questions.other: Most traditional readers see Christ's coming in AD 70 as a judgment-coming that points to a final bodily return (Acts 1:11). Many hold that 24:30 is AD 70 while 24:37-25:46 is the last day. Futurists apply all these to the future. Full preterists apply all to AD 70.

questions.q: How could the judgment of the nations in Matthew 25:31-46 relate to AD 70?
questions.short: This reading does not tie it to one day. It sees Christ, enthroned from his ascension and AD 70 onward, judging nations through history until all enemies are under his feet.
questions.answer: Matthew 25:31 says the Son of Man will sit on his glorious throne and gather the nations. How can that fit a first-century event? This reading says the passage need not describe one moment. Daniel 7:14 gives the Son of Man an everlasting rule over all peoples. Jesus was raised to God's right hand (Acts 2:33-35). He must reign until all enemies are under his feet (1 Corinthians 15:25). Milton Terry wrote that Matthew 25:31-46 does not present one single event. The Psalms say God reigns among the nations and judges the peoples (Psalms 96:10-13). On this reading, the King took his throne in that generation, and his judging of nations continues until he hands the kingdom to the Father (1 Corinthians 15:24).
examples: Psalms 22:28 says the kingdom belongs to the Lord and he rules over the nations.
History shows nations rising and falling under God, such as Rome itself, which fell in the West in AD 476.
questions.other: Most Christian traditions read Matthew 25:31-46 as the last judgment of all people at the bodily return of Christ, with eternal life and eternal punishment (25:46; John 5:28-29). They note the passage ends with final destinies, which they think points beyond ongoing judgment in history.

questions.q: What did Jesus mean when he said it is easier for heaven and earth to pass than for one stroke of the law to fail (Luke 16:17; Matthew 5:18)?
questions.short: On the fulfilled reading, the law would stand until it was fulfilled and its "heaven and earth" passed away. Jesus later said that heaven and earth would pass in that generation.
questions.answer: In Matthew 5:18 Jesus says not one small letter will pass from the law until heaven and earth pass and all is accomplished. Luke 16:16-17 sets this beside "the law and the prophets were until John". On the fulfilled reading, Jesus was saying that the Mosaic order would stand fully until its time was complete. Then he told the disciples that heaven and earth would pass within their generation (Luke 21:32-33). Put together, the law's old covenant order lasted until AD 70, and then passed. John Brown of Edinburgh, commenting on Matthew 5:18, said that Old Testament readers knew the end of the Mosaic order was spoken of as a passing of old heavens and earth.
examples: Matthew 5:17-18: "till heaven and earth pass" is paired with "till all be fulfilled".
Hebrews 7:12: when the priesthood changes, the law must also change.
questions.other: Most readers take "easier for heaven and earth to pass" as a strong way to say "never": the law's moral demand will not fail. Many add that Christ fulfilled the law in his life and death, so the ceremonial parts ended at the cross, while the cosmos remains until the final day.

questions.q: Did the old covenant end at the cross, or did it continue until AD 70?
questions.short: On the fulfilled reading, the old covenant was made old at the cross but was still "vanishing" when Hebrews was written. It fully passed when the temple fell in AD 70.
questions.answer: Jesus' death tore the temple veil (Matthew 27:51) and set up the new covenant in his blood (Luke 22:20). Yet the temple still stood for about forty years. Priests still offered sacrifices. The apostles still went to the temple to pray (Acts 3:1). Hebrews, written while the temple stood, says the first covenant was "becoming old" and "near to vanishing" (Hebrews 8:13). It also says the way into the holy place was not yet open "while the first tabernacle is still standing" (Hebrews 9:8). On the fulfilled reading, the forty years were a time of overlap. The new had come, and the old was passing. When the temple fell, the old covenant's visible world ended, and nothing was left to compete with Christ.
examples: Acts 21:26: Paul took part in temple purification rites about AD 57.
Israel spent forty years in the wilderness between the exodus and the land; AD 30 to AD 70 is also about forty years.
questions.other: Many Reformed and evangelical readers say the old covenant ended at the cross (Colossians 2:14; Ephesians 2:15), and AD 70 was only a visible judgment that confirmed it. Dispensationalists add that God's promises to Israel as a nation remain for the future (Romans 11:26).

questions.q: How did ancient Hebrews understand "heaven and earth"?
questions.short: They used it for the whole created world, but also as a picture. The temple was built as a small cosmos, and the prophets used sky and land for rulers, peoples and covenant orders.
questions.answer: Ancient Israelites had no telescopes or photos from space. "Heaven and earth" for them meant everything God made, seen from the ground: the sky above and the land below (Genesis 1:1). But the phrase also carried more. God's dwelling was "in heaven", and the temple was his house on earth, built in the pattern shown to Moses (Exodus 25:9, 40). So the temple was a picture of heaven and earth together. The prophets also used sky and land for the order of a nation: its kings as lights, its people as land. On the covenantal reading, when a Hebrew heard that heaven and earth would pass, he could think of a world-order ending, not only of the planet.
examples: Psalms 78:69 compares the sanctuary to the heights and to the earth.
Isaiah 66:1: heaven is God's throne and the earth his footstool; the next words ask what house anyone could build for him.
questions.other: Others agree the temple mirrored the cosmos (G. K. Beale, J. Richard Middleton) but conclude the reverse: the temple pointed to God filling the whole physical creation. So the new creation is the whole renewed world becoming God's temple, not only a covenant people.

questions.q: Did Jews of Jesus' time see the tabernacle and temple as a model of heaven and earth?
questions.short: Yes. Josephus, a priest writing about AD 93, said the three parts of the tabernacle stood for land, sea and heaven. Philo said similar things. So "heaven and earth" could describe the temple.
questions.answer: Josephus explained that Moses divided the tabernacle into three parts. Two parts were open to the priests and stood for the land and the sea, which all people can reach. The third, the Most Holy Place, was set apart for God, "because heaven is inaccessible to men" (Antiquities 3.7.7). He also said the temple veil was woven with a picture of the heavens (Jewish War 5.5.4). The outer court and holy place answer to the earth and sea; the inner room answers to heaven. On the covenantal reading, this is how a first-century Jew could think. When Jesus, speaking about the temple, said heaven and earth would pass, his hearers had a ready frame for it: the temple-world of God's covenant would end.
examples: Josephus, Jewish War 5.5.4: the Babylonian veil showed "a panorama of the heavens", except the signs of the zodiac.
Josephus, Antiquities 3.7.7: the twelve loaves stand for the months, and the seven lamps for the planets.
questions.other: Scholars accept the evidence but differ on its use. Many say Josephus shows that the temple symbolized the cosmos, not that "heaven and earth" in Scripture meant the temple. They note Jesus could still contrast his words with the literal cosmos in Matthew 24:35.

questions.q: Does the setting of Matthew 23-24 support reading "heaven and earth" as the temple-world?
questions.short: On the fulfilled reading, strongly yes. The whole talk starts with Jesus leaving the temple, calling it desolate, and predicting its stones would be thrown down.
questions.answer: Matthew 23 ends with woes on the leaders and the words, "Your house is left to you desolate" (23:38). Jesus also says that all the blood of the righteous will come "on this generation" (23:36). In 24:1-2 he leaves the temple and says not one stone will stay on another. The disciples ask when (24:3). The answer ends with "this generation will not pass" and "heaven and earth will pass" (24:34-35). On the fulfilled reading, the whole discourse is about the temple and Jerusalem. To switch at verse 35 to the end of the physical universe would be sudden. It is more natural to read "heaven and earth" as the temple-centred world that the chapter has been describing.
examples: Matthew 23:36 and 24:34 both say "this generation", framing the talk.
The disciples pointed out the temple buildings (Matthew 24:1). Herod's temple was famous for its huge white stones (Josephus, Jewish War 5.5.6).
questions.other: Others note that the disciples' question includes "the end of the age", and Jesus' answer includes the gospel to all nations and the gathering of the elect. They think the talk widens beyond the temple to the final end, so verse 35 can speak of the physical cosmos.

questions.q: How does the new covenant form a "new heaven and new earth"?
questions.short: On the covenantal reading, God replaced each part of the old order: a new priest, sacrifice, temple and people. Together these make a new covenant world, which Scripture can call a new heaven and earth.
questions.answer: James Jordan observed that each time God judged his people in the Old Testament, an old "world" was in a sense replaced: new rulers came and a new symbolic house was built, such as the tabernacle and then the temple. The new covenant does this fully. Christ is the new high priest (Hebrews 7:26-27). His death is the final sacrifice (Hebrews 10:12). His body is the new temple (John 2:19-21). The Word "tabernacled" among us (John 1:14). The church is God's temple (1 Corinthians 3:16; Ephesians 2:21). On this reading, these changes are what Isaiah meant by God creating new heavens and a new earth. The old temple-world passed, and a new one in Christ took its place.
examples: John 2:19-21: "Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up" — he spoke of his body.
Ephesians 2:19-22: Jews and Gentiles are built together into a holy temple in the Lord.
questions.other: Most traditional readers agree that Christ and the church are the new temple. But they see this as the first stage of new creation. They expect the full stage when God renews the whole world and dwells with his people bodily (Romans 8:19-23; Revelation 21:3).

questions.q: Is Genesis 1 itself about God's covenant people rather than the physical universe?
questions.short: One covenantal reading says Genesis 1 speaks mainly of God forming a covenant people. Most covenantal readers stop short of this and accept Genesis 1 as the physical creation, while seeing it as temple-building.
questions.answer: One form of the covenantal reading argues that "the heavens and the earth" in Genesis 1 point first to God's covenant people. It notes that "host" in Genesis 2:1 can mean an army of people, and that "generations" in Genesis 2:4 is used for family lines. It also notes that later prophets reuse Genesis 1 for Israel's birth and judgment (Jeremiah 4:23). On this reading, the "first heaven and first earth" of Revelation 21:1 is the old covenant creation that began in Eden. A milder form says Genesis 1 is the real creation, told as the building of a cosmic temple, and that later Scripture reuses its words for covenant events. Both forms see covenant at the heart of creation.
examples: Genesis 2:15 uses the words "work and keep" for Adam in the garden; Numbers 3:7-8 uses the same pair for Levites in the tabernacle.
Exodus 39:43 echoes Genesis 1:31 and 2:2-3: Moses saw the work, it was done, and he blessed it.
questions.other: Almost all Christian traditions read Genesis 1 as God creating the actual world (Psalms 33:6-9; Hebrews 11:3; John 1:3). Most scholars, including many preterists, think the strong form goes too far. They say Genesis 1 is the base that later covenant uses build on, not itself a covenant picture.

questions.q: Does the "host" of Genesis 2:1 mean an army of people?
questions.short: The Hebrew word tsaba means a host or army. It is used for Israel's tribes, but in Genesis 2:1 most read it as the stars and all creatures. The covenantal reading sees a hint of a people.
questions.answer: Genesis 2:1 says the heavens and the earth were finished, "and all the host of them". The word is tsaba. Its main sense is a large group organised for war. Exodus 6:26 uses the plural of the same word when God brings Israel out of Egypt "by their armies". The covenantal reading sees here a hint that heaven and earth are filled with a people ready for service. A note of care: the paper this idea comes from gives the word as tseba'ah; the standard form is tsaba, with the plural tsevaot, as in "Lord of hosts". In many texts the "host of heaven" is the stars (Deuteronomy 4:19). In others it is angels (1 Kings 22:19). The word fits whatever fills each realm.
examples: "Lord of hosts" (YHWH tsevaot) appears more than 250 times in the Old Testament.
Daniel 8:10 links "the host of heaven" and the stars with God's holy people (8:24).
questions.other: Most scholars say "all their host" in Genesis 2:1 sums up the stars, birds, fish and animals of Genesis 1. They see Daniel 8:10 as a later picture-use, not the meaning of Genesis 2:1. Some agree that "host" carries a military tone of God's ordered creation.

questions.q: Does "the generations of the heavens and the earth" (Genesis 2:4) show that heaven and earth are people?
questions.short: The word toledot, "generations", usually heads a family history. The covenantal reading sees Genesis 2:4 as starting the line of God's people from Adam. Others see it as "what came from" creation.
questions.answer: Genesis is built around headings: "These are the generations of..." (2:4; 5:1; 6:9; 10:1; 11:10; 11:27; 25:12; 25:19; 36:1; 37:2). Nearly all of them introduce people and their descendants. Only the first is "of the heavens and the earth". Genesis 5:1 then says, "This is the book of the generations of Adam." On the covenantal reading, this suggests that the story of heaven and earth is the story of a family: Adam, Noah, Shem, Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, leading to Christ (Luke 3:23-38). God's concern in creation was a people. The phrase in 2:4 introduces Adam, the garden and the covenant command, not more facts about stars.
examples: Genesis 37:2: "These are the generations of Jacob" — the story then follows Joseph and his brothers.
Luke 3:38 traces Jesus' line back to "Adam, the son of God".
questions.other: Most commentators, such as Gordon Wenham, say toledot introduces what came from something. So 2:4 means "this is what came of the heavens and earth", leading into the story of mankind. That supports a people-focus without making heaven and earth themselves a people.

questions.q: Do Zechariah 12:1 and Genesis 2:7 show man as heaven joined to earth?
questions.short: The covenantal reading notes that God made man from dust of the earth and breath from above. Zechariah 12:1 puts the stretching of heaven, the founding of earth, and the forming of man's spirit together.
questions.answer: Zechariah 12:1 introduces a word "concerning Israel" from the Lord who stretched out the heavens, laid the earth's foundation, and formed the human spirit. Genesis 2:7 shows God forming man from the dust of the ground and breathing life into him. The covenantal reading sees a pattern. Earth (dust) and heaven (God's breath) meet in man. Man is a small "heaven and earth", made for covenant life with God. On this reading, it is no surprise that later Scripture calls God's people his heaven and earth. Zechariah uses creation words as the backdrop for a prophecy about Jerusalem and Judah, which fits a covenant use of the phrase.
examples: 1 Corinthians 15:47-49: the first man was "of the earth", the second man "from heaven".
Isaiah 42:5 also joins creating the heavens, spreading the earth, and giving breath to people.
questions.other: Most readers see Zechariah 12:1 as a normal title of God as Creator. It stresses his power to do what the prophecy says. They agree man joins dust and breath but would not draw from this that "heaven and earth" in general means people.

questions.q: Does the Bible ever use "heaven and earth" for the physical world?
questions.short: Yes, often. Both readings agree. The covenantal reading only claims that many texts also use the phrase as a picture of a people or a covenant order, so context must decide.
questions.answer: Genesis 1:1 tells of God making the world. Psalms 121:2 says help comes from the Lord who made heaven and earth. Acts 4:24 and 14:15 praise God as Maker of heaven, earth and sea. Jeremiah 10:11-13 contrasts the idols, who did not make heaven and earth, with the Lord who made the earth by his power and brings rain and wind. These are about the real created world. The covenantal reading accepts this. Its point is that Scripture also uses the same words in a covenant way, as in Deuteronomy 32:1 or Isaiah 51:16. The same phrase can mean different things. Readers must ask each time what the context shows.
examples: Jeremiah 10:11 is written in Aramaic, the only Aramaic verse in Jeremiah. It was a message for the nations: their gods did not make heaven and earth.
Acts 17:24: God who made the world does not live in temples made by hands.
questions.other: Traditional readers agree the phrase can be figurative. They argue that the physical sense is the normal one, and the figurative sense needs clear signals in the text. They say "heaven and earth will pass away" has no such signal and naturally means the created world.

questions.q: Did Moses call the physical universe to witness against Israel (Deuteronomy 4:26; 30:19; 31:28)?
questions.short: The covenantal reading says Moses was speaking in covenant language. Heaven and earth were the formal witnesses of Israel's covenant, and the phrase also pictures Israel itself. Lifeless matter cannot testify.
questions.answer: Moses said, "I call heaven and earth to witness against you today" (Deuteronomy 4:26; 30:19; 31:28). Can sky and soil give testimony? In the ancient world, treaties named witnesses. Hittite treaties listed the gods and also "heaven and earth, mountains and rivers". Israel had no other gods to call, so Moses called heaven and earth. On the covenantal reading, this shows that "heaven and earth" belong to covenant language. They are tied to Israel's covenant and its blessings and curses. One form of this reading says the witnesses are the people themselves, the covenant heaven and earth. Either way, the words point to covenant, not to astronomy.
examples: Joshua 24:27: Joshua set up a stone and said it had "heard" all the Lord's words and would be a witness.
Hittite vassal treaties (about 1400-1200 BC) end with lists of witnesses including heaven and earth.
questions.other: Most scholars see personification: heaven and earth are lasting parts of creation that "watch" the covenant, as in Joshua 24:27. They agree it is covenant language, but say it uses the physical world as witness rather than meaning the people of Israel.

questions.q: Whom did Moses address in "Give ear, O heavens... hear, O earth" (Deuteronomy 32:1)?
questions.short: The covenantal reading says Moses was speaking to Israel, gathered in front of him. The sky and soil have no ears. Israel was God's covenant heaven and earth.
questions.answer: Moses spoke the song "in the ears of all the assembly of Israel" (Deuteronomy 31:30). Right before it, he said he would call heaven and earth to witness against the elders (31:28). Then the song starts: "Give ear, O heavens... hear, O earth" (32:1). The listeners were Israel. On the covenantal reading, Moses used heaven and earth as a name for the people who stood there under covenant. The song then tells Israel's story: God chose them as his portion (32:9), formed them in the wilderness (32:10-11), and would judge them in the latter days (31:29; 32:20-25). Isaiah begins the same way: "Hear, O heavens; give ear, O earth" (Isaiah 1:2), and then speaks to rebel children.
examples: Deuteronomy 31:30 and 32:1 sit side by side: the hearers are Israel, the address is heaven and earth.
Isaiah 1:2: "Hear, O heavens... I have raised children and they have rebelled against me."
questions.other: Most interpreters say Moses and Isaiah used a courtroom form: calling creation as witness while speaking to Israel. Heaven and earth are the jury, not the defendant. They see this as poetry about real creation watching, not a code name for Israel.

questions.q: Does the Song of Moses describe Israel's birth with the words of Genesis 1?
questions.short: Yes. Deuteronomy 32:10-11 uses tohu, "waste", and rachaph, "hover", two words from Genesis 1:2. The covenantal reading sees God "creating" Israel as a covenant heaven and earth.
questions.answer: Deuteronomy 32:10 says God found Jacob in a desert land, in a "waste" (tohu), a howling wilderness. Genesis 1:2 says the earth was tohu, "without form". Deuteronomy 32:11 compares God to an eagle that "hovers" (rachaph) over its young. Genesis 1:2 says the Spirit "hovered" (rachaph) over the waters. These two are the only uses of rachaph in this sense in the Pentateuch. On the covenantal reading, Moses tells Israel's rescue as a new creation. As God shaped the world out of emptiness, he shaped a nation out of slaves in the wilderness. So at the start of the Torah age, God formed a covenant heaven and earth.
examples: Genesis 1:2: tohu (formless) and rachaph (hovered). Deuteronomy 32:10-11: tohu (waste) and rachaph (hovers).
Exodus 19:4: God carried Israel "on eagles' wings" to himself at Sinai.
questions.other: Most scholars accept these echoes and agree the exodus is told as a new creation. They see this as a theme that honours the original creation, not as evidence that "heaven and earth" means Israel. Wider Scripture still places Israel within a physical world God made.

questions.q: How does the eagle of Deuteronomy 32:11 relate to Jesus' hen gathering her chicks (Matthew 23:37)?
questions.short: Both pictures show God sheltering Israel like a parent bird, and both stand in "last days" judgment settings. The covenantal reading links them: Jesus mourns over the nation Moses sang about.
questions.answer: In Deuteronomy 32:11 God is like an eagle stirring its nest, spreading its wings and carrying its young. This is God forming Israel. The same song warns of what will happen "in the latter days" (31:29) and promises vengeance on a perverse generation (32:5, 20). In Matthew 23:37 Jesus says he longed to gather Jerusalem's children like a hen gathers her chicks, but they would not. Then he says their house is left desolate (23:38). On the covenantal reading, the bird image frames the life of the nation from its "creation" at the exodus to its end in Jesus' generation. The heaven and earth that Moses addressed is the world Jesus said would pass.
examples: Deuteronomy 32:5 calls Israel "a perverse and crooked generation"; Peter uses the same phrase in Acts 2:40 for his hearers.
Psalms 91:4: God covers his people with his feathers, under his wings.
questions.other: Others agree the image of a sheltering bird links the texts but say it shows God's love and grief, not that "heaven and earth" in Matthew 24:35 means Israel. Many stress that God's care for Israel continues and that Paul still hopes for Israel's salvation (Romans 11:25-29).

questions.q: Would the sky reveal a wicked man's sin and the ground rise up against him (Job 20:27)?
questions.short: The covenantal reading says no physical sky or soil does this. It is a picture of God and his people bringing a person's guilt to light and opposing him.
questions.answer: Zophar says of the wicked man: the heavens will reveal his guilt, and the earth will rise up against him (Job 20:27). The physical sky cannot speak, and dirt cannot stand up. So this is figurative speech. On the covenantal reading, it shows how the Bible uses "heaven and earth" for something other than the material world. It may mean the courts of heaven and the community on earth. A wicked man is exposed before God and opposed by the people around him. The image appears in a speech full of other pictures, such as fire not blown by man (20:26). The text does not mean that matter has a will.
examples: Genesis 4:10: Abel's blood "cries out" from the ground — a picture of guilt calling for justice.
Habakkuk 2:11: a stone in the wall and a beam in the house cry out against the oppressor.
questions.other: Others agree it is poetry but say it uses real creation to stress that guilt cannot hide anywhere. In Job, God later speaks about the actual sky, sea and animals (Job 38-41). They see figurative use of nature, not evidence that "heaven and earth" means people.

questions.q: Why did God compare Abraham's descendants to stars and to dust?
questions.short: Stars are in heaven, dust is on earth. The covenantal reading says that from Abraham on, God pictured his covenant people as "heaven and earth": the stars of heaven and the dust of the earth.
questions.answer: God told Abraham his seed would be like the dust of the earth (Genesis 13:16). Later he told him to count the stars, and said, "So shall your seed be" (Genesis 15:5). After Abraham offered Isaac, God swore to multiply his seed like the stars of heaven and the sand of the sea (Genesis 22:17). He told Isaac the same (Genesis 26:4). Moses reminded God of this oath (Exodus 32:13). On the covenantal reading, God laid the ground for calling his people heaven and earth. The stars stand for the people in their heavenly calling. The dust stands for them as earthly. Together they are God's covenant "heaven and earth".
examples: Genesis 15:5-6: Abraham believed God about the stars, and God counted it as righteousness. Paul uses this in Romans 4:3.
Daniel 12:3: the wise will shine like the stars forever.
questions.other: Most readers see stars and dust as pictures of a number beyond counting, not as a theory that God's people are "heaven and earth". They agree it is covenant language, and note that Paul says the promised seed is Christ and those in him (Galatians 3:16, 29).

questions.q: Was the promise of descendants like the stars fulfilled before Israel entered the land?
questions.short: Yes. Moses told Israel that they were already "as the stars of heaven for multitude" (Deuteronomy 1:10; 10:22). Nehemiah later said the same. The covenant "heaven" had been filled.
questions.answer: Seventy people went down to Egypt (Genesis 46:27). By the exodus, Israel had about 600,000 men (Exodus 12:37). Moses said, "The Lord your God has multiplied you, and you are today like the stars of heaven" (Deuteronomy 1:10). He repeated it: your fathers went down as seventy, and now God has made you as the stars (Deuteronomy 10:22). Nehemiah 9:23 says God made their children as many as the stars and brought them into the land. On the covenantal reading, this shows how the star picture was used. It was not about astronomy. It was about a people. When God fills his "heaven" with stars, he is filling his covenant with a people.
examples: Genesis 46:27 and Exodus 1:5: seventy persons of Jacob's house came to Egypt.
Numbers 1:46 counts 603,550 fighting men at Sinai.
questions.other: Others agree it was fulfilled in that way but note that the promise also points further. Paul and Hebrews link Abraham's countless seed to all nations who believe (Romans 4:16-18; Hebrews 11:12). They see this as a number-image, not a sign that the sky means Israel.

questions.q: What did Joseph's dream of the sun, moon and eleven stars mean?
questions.short: Jacob knew at once: the sun and moon were himself and Joseph's mother, and the eleven stars were Joseph's brothers. The heavenly lights stood for the family of Israel.
questions.answer: Joseph dreamed that the sun, the moon and eleven stars bowed to him (Genesis 37:9). Jacob did not need an interpreter. He asked, "Shall I and your mother and your brothers bow down to you?" (37:10). The covenantal reading notes this carefully. In the family of promise, the lights of heaven were a picture of the covenant household. The father was the sun, the mother the moon, and the sons the stars. Years later the dream came true when the brothers bowed in Egypt (Genesis 42:6). Revelation 12:1 uses the same picture: a woman clothed with the sun, with the moon under her feet and twelve stars on her head, standing for Israel as God's people.
examples: Genesis 42:6: Joseph's brothers bowed with their faces to the ground before him in Egypt.
Revelation 12:1-5: the woman with sun, moon and twelve stars gives birth to the male child who rules the nations.
questions.other: All readers accept that the dream used heavenly lights as symbols. Traditional readers say the dream was a symbolic vision, so it shows that sky images can stand for people in dreams and visions. They do not see it as proof that "heaven and earth" means Israel in plain statements.

questions.q: Do the physical heavens "utter speech" (Psalms 19:1-4)?
questions.short: Not with words. The psalm itself says there is no speech or language. The covenantal reading says the "heavens" that pour out words are also a picture of God's people spreading his message.
questions.answer: Psalms 19:1-2 says the heavens tell God's glory, and day after day they pour out speech. Verse 3 adds that there is no speech or words, and no voice is heard. Verse 4 says their line goes out through all the earth, and their words to the end of the world. The writer speaks of "their words" and "in them". The covenantal reading asks: can sky and stars really speak? It answers that the psalm uses the heavens as a picture. The second half of the psalm (19:7-11) praises God's law. So the psalm joins creation and covenant. On this reading, the heavens that speak point to a people who carry God's word. Paul confirms this use in Romans 10:18.
examples: Psalms 19:3 in Hebrew can be read "there is no speech... their voice is not heard": silent speech.
Psalms 19:7-11 turns from the sun to the law of the Lord, which revives the soul.
questions.other: Most readers say Psalm 19 describes the silent witness of the real sky, which "speaks" by showing God's power to everyone (Romans 1:20). They see the psalm as moving from God's word in creation (verses 1-6) to his word in Scripture (verses 7-14), both real and both glorious.

questions.q: Who declares God's glory: the stars, or God's people?
questions.short: Both readings agree creation shows his glory. The covenantal reading stresses that Paul quotes Psalms 19:4 for preachers of the gospel, so God's people are the "heavens" whose voice goes to all the earth.
questions.answer: In Romans 10:14-18 Paul asks how people will hear without a preacher. Then he asks, "Have they not heard?" and quotes Psalms 19:4: their voice went out to all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world. Paul applies the words of the "heavens" to the messengers of Christ. On the covenantal reading, this is the key. The New Testament itself reads Psalm 19 about a people who declare God's glory. Psalms 96:3 also tells God's people to declare his glory among the nations. Isaiah 43:21 says God formed a people to declare his praise. So the heavens declare God's glory most clearly when his people speak.
examples: Romans 10:18 quotes Psalms 19:4 word for word from the Greek Old Testament, applied to gospel preachers.
Colossians 1:23: the gospel had been preached "to every creature under heaven" by about AD 60.
questions.other: Many commentators say Paul borrows the psalm's words as an analogy: as the sky's witness is everywhere, so the gospel has gone everywhere. They do not think Paul is saying the heavens in Psalm 19 meant preachers. Paul elsewhere says creation itself shows God (Romans 1:20).

questions.q: Is the sun coming out like a bridegroom (Psalms 19:4-6) a picture of Christ?
questions.short: The covenantal reading sees a prophetic hint of Christ the bridegroom and the "sun of righteousness". Others see a poetic picture of the real sun's daily course.
questions.answer: Psalms 19:4-5 says God set a tent for the sun, which comes out like a bridegroom from his room and runs its course like a strong man. Nothing is hidden from its heat. The covenantal reading notes the bridegroom image. Jesus calls himself the bridegroom (Matthew 9:15). Malachi 4:2 speaks of the sun of righteousness rising with healing. Zechariah, John the Baptist's father, spoke of the "dayspring from on high" visiting us (Luke 1:78). On this reading, Psalm 19 uses the sun to speak of the coming Messiah who brings light to all. The "tent" set for the sun matches God's tabernacle among his people. The psalm is creation language used for covenant purposes.
examples: Malachi 4:2: "the Sun of righteousness shall arise with healing in his wings" (KJV).
Matthew 17:2: at the transfiguration Jesus' face shone like the sun.
questions.other: Most scholars see verses 4-6 as praise for the actual sun, using a bridegroom and a runner to show its joy and strength. Some Christian writers since the Church Fathers saw Christ in it by analogy, but not as the psalm's main sense.

questions.q: Does the covenantal reading deny that the physical heavens show God's glory?
questions.short: No. Its supporters say the physical world is glorious and shows God's power. They only argue that many "heaven and earth" texts use creation as a picture of a greater covenant glory.
questions.answer: The covenantal reading does not deny creation. Its writers say they praise God for the stars, the sea and the land. Romans 1:20 says God's power and nature are clearly seen in what he made. Psalms 8:3 marvels at the moon and stars. Job 38-41 shows God pointing Job to the real sky, sea and animals. The covenantal reading claims something extra. In many passages, the focus is not the physical world but what it pictures: God's relationship with his people. On this reading, creation's glory points to a greater glory, the new creation in Christ (2 Corinthians 4:6). The God who said "Let light shine" has shone in our hearts.
examples: 2 Corinthians 4:6: Paul links "light shall shine out of darkness" (Genesis 1:3) with the light of the gospel in the heart.
Psalms 8:3-4: "When I consider your heavens... what is man?"
questions.other: Critics worry that the reading drifts toward treating the material world as unimportant. They point out that God called creation "very good" (Genesis 1:31), raised Jesus bodily (Luke 24:39), and promises that creation itself will be set free (Romans 8:21). They think the future of matter matters too.

questions.q: Do fish and whales praise the Lord (Psalms 69:34)?
questions.short: The covenantal reading says no in a literal sense. Psalms 69:34-35 calls heaven, earth and seas to praise "for God will save Zion". It is God's saved people who praise him.
questions.answer: Psalms 69:30 begins with one person: "I will praise the name of God with a song." Verse 34 then says, "Let heaven and earth praise him, the seas and everything that moves in them." Verse 35 gives the reason: "For God will save Zion and build the cities of Judah." On the covenantal reading, it would be odd for sea creatures to praise God for saving Zion. Those who praise are those who love God and belong to him. Verse 36 says the children of his servants will inherit the land. So heaven, earth and sea in this psalm picture the people of God, near and far, who rejoice in his salvation.
examples: Psalms 69:32: "The humble shall see this and be glad"; the praise comes from God's people.
Isaiah 60:5 calls the nations "the abundance of the sea" coming to Zion.
questions.other: Most readers say creatures "praise" God by being what he made them to be, as Psalm 148 calls sea monsters, hail and trees to praise him. Revelation 5:13 has every creature in sea and earth praising the Lamb. They see this as real creation joining in, not only a picture of people.

questions.q: What is God's glory "above the heavens" in Psalms 113:4-6?
questions.short: God is higher than all nations and all the heavens, yet he bends down to look at heaven and earth. The covenantal reading recalls the pillar of cloud and fire over Israel.
questions.answer: Psalms 113:4 says the Lord is high above all nations, and his glory above the heavens. Verses 5-6 say he lives on high, yet humbles himself to see what is in heaven and on earth. Verses 7-9 tell of him lifting the poor from the dust and giving the childless woman a home. On the covenantal reading, the psalm sets "heaven and earth" in the setting of God's care for his people. It also recalls the exodus, when God's glory went above Israel in the cloud by day and the fire by night (Exodus 13:21). The God above all comes down to save the lowly. That is covenant, not astronomy.
examples: Exodus 40:34-38: the cloud of glory covered and filled the tabernacle.
Psalms 113:7-8: God lifts the poor from the dust and seats them with princes.
questions.other: Most readers see the psalm as praising God as higher than the whole universe and yet close to the humble. They agree it stresses covenant mercy, but read "heaven and earth" in verse 6 as the whole created order under his eye.

questions.q: How are heaven and earth God's "servants" (Psalms 119:89-91)?
questions.short: The psalm says God's word is fixed in heaven, he established the earth, and "all things are your servants". The covenantal reading sees covenant faithfulness to his people. The natural sense is creation obeying God's laws.
questions.answer: Psalms 119:89 says God's word is settled in heaven forever. Verse 90 says his faithfulness lasts through all generations, and he established the earth so it stands. Verse 91 says they continue to this day by his ordinances, for all are his servants. The covenantal reading notes that "faithfulness" and "generations" are covenant words. Heaven and earth serve God as his people serve him. It also links the "ordinances" to the fixed order God swore by in Jeremiah 31:35-36. A careful reader will note that this same reasoning shows the physical earth "abides". So the psalm supports the view that the material world continues, while God's word governs both creation and covenant.
examples: Jeremiah 33:25 calls the order of day and night God's "covenant" with heaven and earth.
Psalms 104:4 calls wind and fire God's servants.
questions.other: Most commentators read this as creation obeying God's set laws, which shows that his word can be trusted. They say "servants" means creation does his will, as in Psalms 104:4 and 148:8.

questions.q: Who declares God's righteousness (Psalms 50:4-6; 97:6; 22:31)?
questions.short: The heavens, in Psalm 50, and also a people yet to be born, in Psalm 22. The covenantal reading says Psalm 50 calls heaven and earth to judge "his people", and the declaring is done by God's people.
questions.answer: Psalms 50:4 says God calls to the heavens above and to the earth "that he may judge his people". Verse 5 says, "Gather my saints to me, those who made a covenant with me by sacrifice." Verse 6: "The heavens declare his righteousness." Psalms 97:6 says the heavens declare his righteousness and all peoples see his glory. Psalms 22:31 says they will come and declare his righteousness to a people yet to be born. On the covenantal reading, the setting is a covenant trial. God gathers his covenant people. Those who declare his righteousness are people: the saints and the generations who tell what God has done.
examples: Psalms 50:5: the gathering is of those "who made a covenant with me by sacrifice".
Psalms 22:30-31: a seed will serve him; they will tell the next generation what he has done.
questions.other: Others see heaven and earth in Psalm 50 as witnesses in a court scene, as in Deuteronomy 32:1, while God judges his people. They agree that the covenant is central but say the heavens are called as witnesses, not as the people being judged.

questions.q: What does it mean that the wicked "set their mouth against the heavens" (Psalms 73:9)?
questions.short: The arrogant speak against God and his rule, and their words spread over the land. The covenantal reading sees attacks on God and his covenant people, not on the sky.
questions.answer: Psalms 73:8-9 describes proud people who mock and speak with malice. They set their mouths against the heavens, and their tongues strut through the earth. Nobody speaks against the sky for its own sake. "Heavens" here stands for God and his throne, and "earth" for people and life in the land. On the covenantal reading, the line shows how "heaven and earth" can describe the realm of God and his people. The wicked speak against God above and trouble people below. Verse 10 says "his people" turn to them. The psalm resolves when Asaph goes into "the sanctuary of God" (73:17), the place where heaven and earth meet.
examples: Psalms 73:17: Asaph understood their end only when he went into God's sanctuary.
Revelation 13:6: the beast opens its mouth to blaspheme God, his tabernacle, and those who dwell in heaven.
questions.other: Most readers agree "heavens" here means God and his authority, by a common figure of speech (Luke 15:18). They see it as poetry for pride that reaches up to God and out to all people, not as evidence about the meaning of "heaven and earth" elsewhere.

questions.q: Why should "the heavens rejoice and the earth be glad" (Psalms 96:11; 1 Chronicles 16:31)?
questions.short: Because "the Lord reigns" and is coming to judge the peoples. The covenantal reading says the joy belongs to the nations who hear of God's rule, the people pictured as heaven, earth and sea.
questions.answer: Psalms 96:10 says to tell the nations that the Lord reigns. The world is established, and he will judge the peoples fairly. Verse 11 says let the heavens rejoice and the earth be glad; let the sea roar. Verse 13 says he comes to judge the earth. David first sang this when he brought the ark to Jerusalem (1 Chronicles 16:23-33). On the covenantal reading, the joy is the joy of peoples who learn of God's rule. The call to "say among the nations" shows that people are the focus. The rejoicing heavens and earth picture God's people and the nations brought into his worship.
examples: 1 Chronicles 16:31: "Let the heavens be glad, and let the earth rejoice; let men say among the nations, The Lord reigns."
David brought the ark to Jerusalem about 1000 BC; this song was sung that day.
questions.other: Most readers see the whole creation joining in praise, as rivers clap and hills sing in Psalms 98:8. They link this to Romans 8:21, where creation waits for freedom. They see the joy as both human and cosmic.

questions.q: What heavens and earth "perish" and are changed like a garment (Psalms 102:25-27; Hebrews 1:10-12)?
questions.short: The psalm contrasts God, who stays the same, with heavens and earth that wear out. Hebrews applies it to the Son. The covenantal reading links the "old garment" to the old covenant that was growing old.
questions.answer: Psalms 102:25-26 says God laid the earth's foundation and made the heavens, but they will perish. They will wear out like clothing. Like a robe he will change them. Hebrews 1:10-12 quotes this about the Son. A few chapters later Hebrews uses the same idea: the first covenant is "growing old" and near to vanishing (Hebrews 8:13). On the covenantal reading, the writer of Hebrews tells us which heavens and earth were wearing out. It was the old covenant order. Psalms 102:28 then promises that the children of God's servants will continue. A new people stands when the old order is folded up.
examples: Hebrews 1:11 and 8:13 use the same idea of "growing old" (the Greek verb palaioo).
Jesus spoke of not putting new cloth on an old garment (Matthew 9:16), a picture of the new not patching the old.
questions.other: Most readers see the psalm and Hebrews 1 as speaking of the real created universe, which is temporary next to the eternal Son. They link it to Hebrews 12:27 and 2 Peter 3:10 and expect the cosmos to be changed or renewed at Christ's return.

questions.q: What do Jeremiah 31:35-36 and 33:20-21 mean when they tie God's covenant to the sun, moon and stars?
questions.short: God says his covenant will stand as surely as day and night. If the fixed order of the sky could fail, his promise could fail. The fulfilled reading uses this to say the physical heavens do not pass away.
questions.answer: In Jeremiah 31:31-34 God promises a new covenant. In 31:35-36 he says: if the fixed order of sun, moon and stars departs, then Israel's seed will stop being a nation before him. In 33:20-21 he says: if you can break my covenant with day and night, then you can break my covenant with David.
