Psalms 89:36-37 says David's throne will last like the sun and the moon, the faithful witness in the sky. On the fulfilled reading, two points follow. First, the new covenant and David's throne, now held by Christ, are as lasting as the sky. Second, the physical sky is not about to vanish. So the heaven and earth that passed in Jesus' generation must be the old covenant order.
examples: Luke 1:32-33: the angel says God will give Jesus the throne of David and his kingdom will have no end.
Jeremiah 33:25-26 repeats the oath: if I have not set the fixed laws of heaven and earth, then I will reject David's seed.
questions.other: Dispensationalists read "Israel will not cease to be a nation" as a promise to ethnic Israel, still in force. Covenant theologians apply it to the Israel of God in Christ (Galatians 6:16). Many note that the oath is about God's faithfulness, not a claim that the cosmos never changes.

questions.q: Do the physical heavens and earth come under God's judgment?
questions.short: The covenantal reading says sky and soil do not sin, so they are not judged. When prophets show heavens shaken and earth burned, they speak of peoples and rulers judged by God.
questions.answer: In the prophets, heaven and earth are shaken, darkened, rolled up and burned. Who is judged? Sin belongs to people. Isaiah 13:11 says, right in the middle of the darkened sky, "I will punish the world for its evil and the wicked for their sin." Isaiah 24:5 says the earth is defiled because its people broke the everlasting covenant. On the covenantal reading, the cosmic pictures describe God's judgment on nations and their leaders. The sun and moon are kings and powers. The earth is the people in the land. God does not hold rocks guilty. He judges people, and the prophets use the language of a collapsing world to show how total that judgment is.
examples: Isaiah 13:10-11 puts "stars will not give light" and "I will punish the world for its evil" side by side.
Genesis 3:17: the ground was cursed "because of you" — the curse came on creation because of human sin.
questions.other: Others agree that people, not matter, are guilty. But they say creation suffers because of human sin (Genesis 3:17; Romans 8:20). So creation can be shaken as part of God's judgment on people, and later set free. Its judgment is a side effect, not a punishment for its own sin.

questions.q: Do the physical heavens and earth need to be redeemed?
questions.short: The covenantal reading says redemption is for people, not for stars. Others point to Romans 8:19-22, where creation itself waits to be set free from decay.
questions.answer: Redemption in Scripture means buying back a person from slavery or guilt (Exodus 6:6; Ephesians 1:7). Stars and rocks have not sinned, so they do not need forgiveness. On the covenantal reading, this is why texts about heaven and earth being judged and made new are about people. The Bible's main story is God and the redemption of his people. That fits a covenant new creation better than a remade cosmos. Some covenantal readers take Romans 8:19-22 as speaking of the "creation" of humanity, Jew and Gentile, groaning for the revealing of God's sons. They also note that Paul says "if anyone is in Christ, there is a new creation" (2 Corinthians 5:17).
examples: Ephesians 1:7: in Christ we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of sins.
Colossians 1:23: Paul says the gospel was preached "to every creature (ktisis) under heaven" — the same word as "creation" in Romans 8, used for people.
questions.other: Most interpreters read Romans 8:19-22 as the non-human creation, which was subjected to futility and will share the freedom of God's children. They link this with the bodily resurrection and with "restoration of all things" (Acts 3:21; Colossians 1:20). For them, God redeems people and renews their world.

questions.q: What did Isaiah mean by a darkened sun and a shaken earth in his oracle on Babylon (Isaiah 13:10-13)?
questions.short: He described the fall of Babylon to the Medes in 539 BC. The cosmic words picture the collapse of a world empire, not the end of the universe.
questions.answer: Isaiah 13:1 names the subject: "The burden of Babylon." Verse 10 says the stars, sun and moon will not give their light. Verse 13 says God will shake the heavens and move the earth from its place. Verse 17 names the attackers: the Medes. Verse 19 says Babylon will become like Sodom. On the fulfilled reading, this shows how prophets speak. A real empire fell in history, but the prophet used the language of a dying sky. Note: one argument says the pronoun "her" ("her light", "her place") proves that a people is meant. That is weak. "Her" comes from English and Hebrew grammar. The stronger point is the context, which names Babylon and the Medes.
examples: Babylon fell to Cyrus' Medo-Persian army in October 539 BC (Nabonidus Chronicle; Daniel 5:30-31).
Isaiah 13:17 names the Medes as the attackers, about 150 years before they came.
questions.other: Almost all scholars agree Isaiah 13 is about Babylon's fall and uses figurative cosmic language. Some futurists see a double meaning, with a future end-time Babylon (Revelation 18). Others say Isaiah 13:9-13 widens to the final day of the Lord over the whole world.

questions.q: Did the sky really roll up like a scroll over Edom (Isaiah 34:4), and did the stars go dark over Egypt (Ezekiel 32:7-8)?
questions.short: No. These were judgments on real nations, Edom and Egypt. The prophets used the language of a collapsing sky for the fall of their power.
questions.answer: Isaiah 34:4 says the host of heaven will dissolve, the sky will roll up like a scroll, and the stars will fall like leaves. Verse 5 explains: God's sword will come down on Edom, the people he has judged. Ezekiel 32:2 addresses Pharaoh, king of Egypt. Verses 7-8 say that when God puts him out, he will cover the heavens, darken the stars and the sun, and bring darkness on his land. On the fulfilled reading, the sky did not literally roll up. Edom and Egypt fell. These are the same words Jesus uses in Matthew 24:29 and John uses in Revelation 6:13-14. They describe the end of a nation's order.
examples: Edom was overrun by Arab tribes and the Nabataeans by the 4th century BC (Malachi 1:3-4 already sees it desolate).
Nebuchadnezzar defeated Egypt's power at Carchemish in 605 BC and invaded Egypt about 568 BC.
questions.other: Scholars widely agree that these texts are figurative for historical judgments. Futurists say Revelation 6:13-14 uses the same words for a final, worldwide judgment, so the pattern points to an ultimate fulfilment. Many amillennialists see both a near and an ultimate sense.

questions.q: Who is addressed in "Hear, O heavens, and give ear, O earth" (Isaiah 1:2)?
questions.short: The message is about Judah and Jerusalem (1:1). The covenantal reading says Isaiah, like Moses, calls the covenant people "heaven and earth". Others say he calls creation as a witness.
questions.answer: Isaiah 1:1 says the vision concerns Judah and Jerusalem. Verse 2 begins, "Hear, O heavens, and give ear, O earth, for the Lord has spoken: I raised children, and they rebelled against me." Verse 10 then calls the leaders "rulers of Sodom" and the people "people of Gomorrah". On the covenantal reading, Isaiah copies Moses (Deuteronomy 32:1). He speaks to a covenant nation in the language of heaven and earth. The whole book then moves from the judgment of this old "heaven and earth" to the promise of new heavens and a new earth (Isaiah 65:17; 66:22). The book opens and closes with heaven and earth, and both are about God's people.
examples: Isaiah opens with heaven and earth (1:2) and closes with new heavens and new earth (66:22).
Isaiah 1:10 calls Jerusalem's rulers "rulers of Sodom", a picture-name for a covenant people.
questions.other: Most scholars see a covenant lawsuit: God calls heaven and earth as witnesses, as Moses did, and then charges Israel. The witnesses and the accused are different. This keeps the covenant setting but reads heaven and earth as creation.

questions.q: Why are the heavens, earth, mountains and forests told to sing when God redeems Jacob (Isaiah 44:23; 49:13)?
questions.short: Because God has redeemed and comforted his people. The covenantal reading says the singers are people pictured as heavens, earth, mountains and trees.
questions.answer: Isaiah 44:23 says: sing, O heavens; shout, depths of the earth; break into song, mountains, forest and every tree, "for the Lord has redeemed Jacob". Isaiah 49:13 says: sing, heavens; rejoice, earth; break out, mountains, "for the Lord has comforted his people". The reason for joy each time is the redemption of a people. On the covenantal reading, the ones who sing are those who are saved. Scripture often uses mountains for rulers and kingdoms (Daniel 2:35), and trees for people (Psalms 1:3; Isaiah 61:3). So the whole picture is of God's people rejoicing. Isaiah 55:12 adds that the trees will clap their hands when God's people go out in joy.
examples: Isaiah 61:3: God's people are called "oaks of righteousness, the planting of the Lord".
Daniel 2:35: the stone becomes a great mountain that fills the whole earth — a kingdom.
questions.other: Most commentators say Isaiah calls all creation to join in praise, a common poetic form. They do not think mountains and forests are code for people. Some see the singing creation as a hint that redemption will one day reach the whole world.

questions.q: How do Paul and John use Isaiah 49 (2 Corinthians 6:2; Revelation 7:16-17)?
questions.short: Paul quotes Isaiah 49:8 as "now is the day of salvation". John uses Isaiah 49:10 for the redeemed multitude. The covenantal reading sees Isaiah's rejoicing heavens and earth fulfilled in the first-century church.
questions.answer: Isaiah 49:8 says God answered his Servant in a time of favour and helped him in a day of salvation, to restore the land. Paul quotes it and says "now is the day of salvation" (2 Corinthians 6:2). (One paper cites Isaiah 49:1 here; the quoted verse is 49:8.) Isaiah 49:10 says the people will not hunger or thirst, nor will the sun strike them, for God will lead them to springs of water. Revelation 7:16-17 applies this to those who come out of the great tribulation. On the covenantal reading, the 144,000 from Israel's tribes are the believing remnant, the first fruits, and the great multitude includes the nations. Isaiah's singing heavens and earth (49:13) are these saved people.
examples: 2 Corinthians 6:2 (about AD 56): Paul says Isaiah's day of salvation is "now".
Revelation 14:4 calls the 144,000 "first fruits to God and to the Lamb".
questions.other: Dispensationalists see the 144,000 as Jewish believers in a future tribulation. Many amillennialists see both the 144,000 and the multitude as the whole church seen two ways. Most accept that Paul sees Isaiah 49 fulfilled in the gospel age.

questions.q: Why does Isaiah 51:9-11 join creation, the Red Sea and Zion together?
questions.short: Isaiah tells the exodus as a new creation and promises a second exodus to Zion. The covenantal reading says Hebrews 12 shows that second exodus in the first century.
questions.answer: Isaiah 51:9 calls on the Lord's arm to wake as in days of old. It asks: did you not cut Rahab and pierce the dragon? Rahab is a poetic name for Egypt (Isaiah 30:7; Psalms 87:4). Verse 10 says God dried up the sea and made a road for the redeemed. Verse 11 says the ransomed will return to Zion with singing. Creation words (the deep, the dragon) are used for the exodus. On the covenantal reading, God's acts of creating and redeeming are told in one language. Hebrews 12:18-24 contrasts Mount Sinai with Mount Zion, "the heavenly Jerusalem". Believers had come to Zion. The second exodus was taking place, and a new heaven and earth were being formed.
examples: Psalms 87:4 names "Rahab and Babylon" among the nations: Rahab is Egypt.
Hebrews 12:22: "you have come to Mount Zion, the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem."
questions.other: Most scholars agree Isaiah blends creation and exodus imagery and promises a return from Babylon (538 BC onward). Christian readers widely see a fuller fulfilment in Christ. Traditional readers add that the final fulfilment includes a renewed creation, not only a covenant people.

questions.q: What does God mean by "that I may plant the heavens and lay the foundations of the earth, and say to Zion, You are my people" (Isaiah 51:16)?
questions.short: God links the "planting" of heavens and earth with calling Zion his people. The covenantal reading sees this as the clearest text that God's covenant people are his "heaven and earth".
questions.answer: Isaiah 51:15 says, "I am the Lord your God, who divided the sea." Verse 16 says: I have put my words in your mouth and covered you in the shadow of my hand, to plant the heavens, to found the earth, and to say to Zion, "You are my people." The physical heavens were made long before Israel. So this "planting" must be something God did at the exodus and Sinai, when he gave his words and formed a nation. On the covenantal reading, the heavens and earth here are the covenant order and people formed by God's word. The forming of Israel was God's covenant creation. It was his light to the nations.
examples: Isaiah 51:15-16 ties the planting of the heavens to "divided the sea" — the Red Sea at the exodus.
Deuteronomy 4:32-36: Moses compares Sinai with the day God created man on the earth.
questions.other: Many scholars read verse 16 as God, the Creator of heaven and earth, now acting to restore Zion. The infinitives can mean "I, who planted the heavens". Some see a goal: God plans to "plant" a new heavens and earth in the future (Isaiah 65:17).

questions.q: What heavens "vanish like smoke" and what earth "wears out like a garment" (Isaiah 51:6)?
questions.short: Isaiah says the heavens and earth will vanish and wear out, but God's salvation lasts forever. The covenantal reading links this with Hebrews 8:13, where the old covenant is "growing old" and "ready to vanish".
questions.answer: Isaiah 51:4-5 speaks of a law going out from God and his salvation going out to the peoples. Verse 6 says: lift your eyes to the heavens and look at the earth; the heavens will vanish like smoke, and the earth will wear out like a garment, but my salvation will be forever. On the covenantal reading, the New Testament explains this. Hebrews 8:13 says the first covenant is growing old and ready to vanish. Jesus said no one puts new cloth on an old garment (Matthew 9:16). The old covenant was the garment wearing out. The new covenant, God's lasting salvation, replaced it. The time for this was the first century.
examples: Hebrews 8:13 uses "old", "growing aged" and "near to vanishing" — the same ideas as Isaiah 51:6.
Matthew 9:16-17: new wine needs new wineskins.
questions.other: Most commentators say Isaiah contrasts the temporary universe with God's eternal salvation: even creation will pass, but his saving work will not. They see Hebrews 8:13 as a separate point about the covenant, and think linking the two is a thematic echo, not an explanation.

questions.q: Why does Jeremiah describe Judah's ruin as the earth becoming "formless and empty" (Jeremiah 4:23-26)?
questions.short: Jeremiah uses the exact words of Genesis 1:2, tohu wabohu. The covenantal reading says Judah's fall in 586 BC was the undoing of God's covenant creation.
questions.answer: Jeremiah 4:22 says God's people are foolish and do not know him. Verse 23 says: I looked at the earth, and it was formless and void; at the heavens, and they had no light. Verses 24-26 add shaking mountains, no man, fled birds, and a fruitful land turned to desert. These lines run Genesis 1 backward: light, land, people, birds, fruitful land, all removed. The phrase "formless and void" (tohu wabohu) appears only here and in Genesis 1:2. On the covenantal reading, Jeremiah shows that the judgment of Judah was a "de-creation". The covenant world went back to chaos when Babylon destroyed Jerusalem and the temple in 586 BC.
examples: Genesis 1:2 and Jeremiah 4:23 are the only two places with the full phrase tohu wabohu.
Babylon burned the temple in 586 BC (2 Kings 25:8-9). The sun did not go out, but Judah's world ended.
questions.other: All major views accept the echo of Genesis 1 and agree the passage is about Judah's fall. Traditional readers say this shows how serious sin is, as if creation were undone, but not that Genesis 1 itself is about Israel.

questions.q: Does the earth really mourn and the heavens turn black (Jeremiah 4:28)?
questions.short: Not as feelings in soil or sky. The covenantal reading says it is God's people who mourn when he comes in judgment. The land and sky picture the nation and its leaders.
questions.answer: Jeremiah 4:27 says the whole land will be desolate, yet God will not make a full end. Verse 28 says that for this the earth will mourn and the heavens above be black, because God has spoken and will not turn back. The physical earth does not grieve. On the covenantal reading, the mourning belongs to the people of the land. Joel 1:10 says the ground mourns because the grain is ruined, but then calls the priests to mourn (1:13). Hosea 4:3 says the land mourns because of the people's sin. The darkened heavens picture the fall of the nation's rulers. So "earth" and "heavens" here are the covenant people, mourning under judgment.
examples: Hosea 4:1-3: because there is no faithfulness in the land, the land mourns.
Lamentations 1:4: "the roads of Zion mourn" — the roads stand for the people who no longer travel to the feasts.
questions.other: Others agree this is personification. But they say Scripture shows the land truly suffering from sin, through drought and ruin (Jeremiah 12:4), so "the earth mourns" describes real damage to the land as well as the people's grief.

questions.q: Is Jeremiah 10:11-13 about the physical sky or about God's people?
questions.short: Its plain subject is God as Maker of the real heavens and earth, against idols. One covenantal reading sees hints of Judah's coming trouble, but this passage is mainly about creation.
questions.answer: Jeremiah 10:11 says the gods who did not make the heavens and the earth will perish from the earth. Verses 12-13 say God made the earth by his power and stretched out the heavens by his wisdom. When he speaks, waters roar in the sky, clouds rise, and lightning and wind come. This is about real weather and real creation. One covenantal paper admits it is "difficult language" and links it to the calamity coming on God's people (10:17-22). A careful reading keeps both. The chapter does go on to Judah's exile. But verses 11-13 use "heaven and earth" in its physical sense, to show that the Lord, not the idols, rules the world.
examples: Jeremiah 10:11 is in Aramaic, the language of the nations, so exiles could tell their captors.
Jeremiah 10:17-18 then warns: gather your bundle, for God will throw out the people of the land.
questions.other: Traditional readers use this text as a clear case of "heaven and earth" meaning the physical creation. They see it as a control on figurative readings: the same prophet who used the phrase as a picture in chapter 4 used it plainly here.

questions.q: Why do "the heavens and the earth and all that is in them" sing over Babylon's fall (Jeremiah 51:48)?
questions.short: Because the oppressor of God's people is destroyed. The covenantal reading says those who sing are God's people and the freed nations.
questions.answer: Jeremiah 51:48 says the heavens and the earth and all in them will sing for joy over Babylon, because destroyers come against her from the north. Babylon had destroyed Jerusalem and the temple. Her fall meant freedom for the exiles (Jeremiah 51:45, 50). On the covenantal reading, the joyful heavens and earth are the people released from her power. Revelation 18:20 echoes this: "Rejoice over her, O heaven, you saints and apostles and prophets." There the word "heaven" is explained by "saints, apostles and prophets". The covenantal reading sees this as the Bible's own key to what a rejoicing "heaven" means.
examples: Revelation 18:20 places "heaven" beside "saints and apostles and prophets" as those who rejoice.
Cyrus' decree (538 BC) let the Jewish exiles return home after Babylon fell (Ezra 1:1-4).
questions.other: Most commentators see the line as poetic praise in which creation joins God's people. Some note Revelation 18:20 addresses heaven and then the saints as two groups called to rejoice, rather than defining heaven as the saints.

questions.q: What does Hosea mean when God will "answer the heavens, and they will answer the earth" (Hosea 2:21-23)?
questions.short: In the day God renews his marriage covenant, blessing flows from heaven to earth to grain and to "Jezreel", God's people. The covenantal reading sees heaven and earth tied closely to the covenant people.
questions.answer: Hosea 2:18 says God will make a covenant for his people with the animals, birds and creeping things, and break the bow and sword. Verses 19-20 say he will betroth Israel to himself forever in righteousness and faithfulness. Verses 21-22 say he will answer the heavens, the heavens will answer the earth, the earth will answer the grain, wine and oil, and they will answer Jezreel. Verse 23 says he will sow her in the land and call "Not my people" "my people". On the covenantal reading, heaven and earth here belong inside a covenant renewal. Paul and Peter apply Hosea 2:23 to the church of Jews and Gentiles (Romans 9:25-26; 1 Peter 2:10). The new heaven and earth is this renewed covenant people.
examples: Romans 9:24-26: Paul applies Hosea's "not my people... my people" to Jews and Gentiles called by God.
1 Peter 2:10: once not a people, now God's people.
questions.other: Others see a chain of blessing through real creation: rain from the sky, crops from the soil, food for the people. They say this shows covenant blessing reaching the physical world, which fits a renewed creation as well as a renewed people.

questions.q: What were the "wonders in the heavens and in the earth" in Joel 2:30-31?
questions.short: Peter said Joel's prophecy was being fulfilled at Pentecost (Acts 2:16). The fulfilled reading places the wonders in the land of Israel between Pentecost and the "great day" of AD 70.
questions.answer: Joel 2:28-29 promises the Spirit on all flesh. Verses 30-31 add wonders in the heavens and earth, blood, fire and smoke, the sun dark and the moon blood, before the great day of the Lord. Verse 32 says those who call on the Lord will be saved. Peter quoted this whole text at Pentecost and said, "This is that" (Acts 2:16-21). The sun did not turn dark that morning. On the fulfilled reading, the whole passage covers one span: the gift of the Spirit, signs done by Christ and the apostles (Acts 2:22, 43), and the coming day of judgment on Jerusalem. Peter told his hearers to save themselves "from this crooked generation" (Acts 2:40).
examples: Acts 2:16: "this is that which was spoken by the prophet Joel" (KJV).
Darkness covered the land for three hours at the crucifixion (Luke 23:44-45), some weeks before Pentecost.
questions.other: Many scholars see Pentecost as the start of Joel's fulfilment, with the cosmic signs either figurative or still future before Christ's return. Dispensationalists often hold that Joel will be fully fulfilled in the future tribulation, and that Pentecost was a partial fulfilment.

questions.q: What does Habakkuk mean by "his glory covered the heavens, and the earth was full of his praise" (Habakkuk 3:3)?
questions.short: Habakkuk recalls God coming from Teman and Paran, as at Sinai. The covenantal reading says praise comes from people, so the earth "full of praise" is God's people.
questions.answer: Habakkuk 3:3 says God came from Teman, the Holy One from Mount Paran. His glory covered the heavens, and the earth was full of his praise. These places lie south, on the route of Israel's wilderness journey (Deuteronomy 33:2). The prayer recalls God's coming at Sinai and the exodus, then looks to future salvation (3:13). On the covenantal reading, who praises God but his people? Earth "full of praise" means a land filled with worshippers. Habakkuk 2:14 also promises that the earth will be filled with the knowledge of God's glory as the waters cover the sea. That is about people knowing God.
examples: Deuteronomy 33:2: the Lord came from Sinai, rose from Seir, and shone from Mount Paran.
Habakkuk 2:14 echoes Isaiah 11:9: the earth full of the knowledge of the Lord.
questions.other: Most commentators read this as a theophany: God's brightness fills the sky and his praise is heard across the world. They agree praise comes from people but read "earth" as the world in which they live.

questions.q: What is the shaking of "the heavens and the earth" in Haggai 2:6-7 and Hebrews 12:26-28?
questions.short: Hebrews says the shaking removes what can be shaken so that an unshakable kingdom remains. The fulfilled reading sees the old covenant order removed in the first century and the kingdom of Christ standing.
questions.answer: Haggai 2:6-7 says that "once more, in a little while" God will shake heaven, earth, sea and dry land, and all nations, and fill his house with glory. Hebrews 12:26-27 quotes this and says "once more" shows the removal of things that are shaken, so that what cannot be shaken may remain. Verse 28 says "we are receiving a kingdom that cannot be shaken." The verb is present tense. On the fulfilled reading, the readers stood between Sinai and Zion (12:18-24). The thing being shaken and removed was the old covenant world. The kingdom being received was Christ's. John Owen and Milton Terry both linked this shaking with the fall of the Jewish state.
examples: Hebrews 12:28: "we are receiving" (present tense) a kingdom that cannot be shaken.
Haggai spoke in 520 BC when the second temple was being built (Haggai 1:1; 2:3).
questions.other: Many commentators read Hebrews 12:26-27 as the final shaking of the created order at Christ's return, after which only the eternal kingdom remains. Others see a two-stage fulfilment: Christ's first coming and AD 70 began it, and the final day completes it.

questions.q: Why did God tell Zerubbabel, "I will shake the heavens and the earth" (Haggai 2:21-22)?
questions.short: Because he would overthrow thrones and kingdoms. The text itself explains the shaking as the fall of nations' power, not of the physical sky.
questions.answer: Haggai 2:21 says to Zerubbabel, the governor of Judah, that God will shake the heavens and the earth. Verse 22 explains: he will overthrow the thrones of kingdoms, destroy the strength of the nations, and overturn chariots and riders. Verse 23 makes Zerubbabel, David's heir, like a signet ring. On the fulfilled reading, the shaking of heaven and earth is defined right there as political upheaval. Kingdoms fall, and David's line is kept. This prepares for Christ, son of Zerubbabel (Matthew 1:12-13), whose kingdom cannot be shaken (Hebrews 12:28). Both Haggai texts use "heaven and earth" for world powers, not for stars.
examples: Matthew 1:12-16 lists Zerubbabel in the line of Jesus.
After Haggai (520 BC), Persia fell to Alexander (331 BC), and his empire split among his generals.
questions.other: Most scholars agree that the shaking here is political. They see it as part of God's rule in history and as pointing to the Messiah. Some still read Hebrews' use of Haggai as including a final cosmic shaking.

questions.q: Why does Peter tell his readers to remember "the words spoken before by the holy prophets" (2 Peter 3:1-2)?
questions.short: Because his hope of new heavens and a new earth came from the prophets, especially Isaiah. The fulfilled reading says Peter taught nothing new, so his words must be read in the prophets' covenant sense.
questions.answer: Peter says he writes to stir their minds to remember the prophets' words and the apostles' command (2 Peter 3:1-2). Paul said he taught nothing except what the prophets and Moses said would happen (Acts 26:22). Peter's readers knew the phrase "new heavens and new earth" from Isaiah 65:17 and 66:22. On the fulfilled reading, Peter directs them back to these texts on purpose. In Isaiah the new heavens and earth come with a new Jerusalem, a people who rejoice, and the judgment of rebels. So Peter's picture of fire and new creation should be read in the same way: the end of one covenant world and the full arrival of another.
examples: Acts 26:22: Paul says he said nothing beyond what the prophets and Moses foretold.
Isaiah 65:17 and 66:22 are the only Old Testament texts that say "new heavens and a new earth".
questions.other: Others agree Peter draws on Isaiah but say that he, like Isaiah, describes a real renewal of the world. They note that later Jewish writings, such as 1 Enoch 91:16, also read Isaiah's promise as a cosmic renewal, which suggests Peter's readers could hear it that way.

questions.q: Who were the mockers asking "Where is the promise of his coming?" (2 Peter 3:3-4)?
questions.short: On the fulfilled reading, they were people in the 60s AD who saw the promised generation running out and doubted Jesus' word. The fall of Jerusalem in AD 70 answered them.
questions.answer: Peter says scoffers will come in the last days, asking where the promise of his coming is, since all things continue as they were (2 Peter 3:3-4). Jesus had said some standing with him would see him come in his kingdom (Matthew 16:27-28), and that this generation would see all these things (Matthew 24:34). The apostles taught his coming was near (Philippians 4:5; James 5:8; 1 John 2:18). On the fulfilled reading, by the mid-60s, over thirty years had passed. Some began to scoff. Peter answers that God is not slow (3:9). The mockers matched Jesus' servant who said, "My master delays" (Matthew 24:48). The events of AD 70 then silenced such doubts.
examples: 2 Peter was likely written about AD 64-68, before Peter's death under Nero.
James 5:8-9: "The coming of the Lord is at hand... the judge stands at the door."
questions.other: Most interpreters say the mockers deny Christ's final return in any age, and that Peter's answer ("a day is like a thousand years", 3:8) explains a long delay. They see the scoffers' claim that "all things continue" as a denial of God's intervention in history generally.

questions.q: Did the flood destroy the physical heavens (2 Peter 3:5-6)?
questions.short: No. The sky and the planet remained after the flood. Peter says "the world that then was" perished. The covenantal reading concludes that the "heavens of old" were a people and their world-order.
questions.answer: Peter says that by God's word the heavens existed long ago, and the earth was formed out of water and by water. By these, "the world that then was" was flooded and perished (2 Peter 3:5-6). Whether the flood was global or regional, the sky was not destroyed. The same sun rose on Noah after the flood (Genesis 8:22). On the covenantal reading, what perished was people: the corrupt line described in Genesis 6:1-7. Peter uses "world" (kosmos) for the world of the ungodly (2 Peter 2:5). If the flood's "heavens and earth" can perish without the stars ending, then the coming fire on the present "heavens and earth" can do the same.
examples: 2 Peter 2:5: God did not spare "the world of the ungodly" (kosmos asebon) but saved Noah.
Genesis 8:22: after the flood God promises seedtime and harvest, day and night, will not cease.
questions.other: Many commentators reply that the flood truly ruined the physical earth's surface and life, which is why Peter calls it destruction. They say Peter's point is that God has judged the physical world before and will do it again by fire, so the parallel supports a real cosmic event.

questions.q: What are "the heavens and the earth which are now" (2 Peter 3:7)?
questions.short: On the covenantal reading, they were the covenant world that began after the flood with Noah, ran through Abraham and Moses, and stood in Peter's day. It was "kept for fire".
questions.answer: Peter contrasts the world that perished in the flood with "the heavens and earth that now are", kept by the same word for fire on the day of judgment of ungodly people (2 Peter 3:7). God promised Noah he would not destroy the earth again by flood (Genesis 9:11). Through Shem and then Abraham the covenant line went on. At Sinai, God formed Israel as a nation. On the covenantal reading, this whole covenant order, centred finally on the temple, was the "heavens and earth which are now". It was reserved for judgment. The fire fell on that world when Jerusalem and the temple burned. The judgment Peter names is the destruction of "ungodly people", not of planets.
examples: Genesis 9:11: God promises never again to destroy the earth with a flood.
Josephus describes the temple burning in AD 70, and the city later set on fire (Jewish War 6.4.5-7; 6.8.5).
questions.other: Most readers see "the heavens and earth that now are" as the present physical world, which God will judge at the last day. They note Peter compares the flood with fire to show the scale of judgment, and that he expects ungodly people everywhere to face it, not only in Judea.

questions.q: What "heavens" were judged by fire soon after Peter wrote?
questions.short: On the fulfilled reading, the temple and Jerusalem, the centre of the old covenant world. Roman soldiers burned the temple in AD 70, within a few years of Peter's letter.
questions.answer: If Peter wrote about AD 64-68, the next great fire on God's people came very soon. The Roman general Titus took Jerusalem in AD 70. Josephus tells that a soldier threw a burning brand into the temple, and the fire spread through it (Jewish War 6.4.5). Later the Romans set fire to the city (6.8.5). The priesthood and sacrifices ended. On the fulfilled reading, this was the "fire" Peter warned of. Malachi had spoken of a day burning like an oven (Malachi 4:1). John the Baptist warned of chaff burned with fire (Matthew 3:12). Jesus told of a king who sent troops and burned their city (Matthew 22:7). Each points to AD 70.
examples: Matthew 22:7: in the wedding parable, the king sends armies, destroys the murderers and burns their city.
Josephus, Jewish War 6.4.5: the temple burned on the 10th of the month Lous (Ab), August AD 70.
questions.other: Partial preterists such as Kenneth Gentry argue that 2 Peter 3 is the final consummation, not AD 70, because it speaks of the whole creation and of the destruction of ungodly people generally. Futurists and amillennialists agree. Some, such as John Owen, did read 2 Peter 3 as AD 70.

questions.q: What are the "elements" that melt with fervent heat (2 Peter 3:10, 12)?
questions.short: The Greek word stoicheia can mean physical elements, heavenly bodies, or basic principles. The fulfilled reading notes Paul uses it for the "elements" of the old law (Galatians 4:3, 9), and applies Peter's text to the old covenant order.
questions.answer: Peter says the elements will melt with burning heat (2 Peter 3:10, 12). The word stoicheia means the basic parts of something. In Greek writing it can mean earth, air, fire and water. It can also mean the heavenly bodies. In the New Testament it is used for basic principles: "the weak and beggarly elements" Paul's readers wanted to return to (Galatians 4:9), "the elements of the world" (Colossians 2:8, 20), and "the first principles of God's word" (Hebrews 5:12). On the fulfilled reading, Peter speaks of the old covenant's elements: its rituals, sacrifices and temple order. They "melted" in the fire of AD 70. Peter's readers had been warned not to cling to them.
examples: Galatians 4:3, 9: Paul calls the old law's rules "elements" (stoicheia) that enslave.
Hebrews 5:12: "the first principles (stoicheia) of the oracles of God".
questions.other: Most scholars say that in a passage about heavens, earth, fire and melting, stoicheia means the physical parts of the universe or the heavenly bodies, as in Isaiah 34:4 (Greek version). Richard Bauckham notes the word often meant heavenly bodies in this setting.

questions.q: What does "the earth and the works in it will be burned up" mean (2 Peter 3:10)?
questions.short: One covenantal reading sees the "works" as the works of the law and the temple that burned in AD 70. The oldest Greek copies read "will be found" or "laid bare", pointing to exposure in judgment.
questions.answer: The KJV says the earth and the works in it "shall be burned up" (2 Peter 3:10). The oldest manuscripts, Sinaiticus and Vaticanus, read heurethesetai, "will be found". Many modern versions say "laid bare" or "exposed". This means all deeds will be uncovered before God. On one covenantal reading, the "works" are the works of the law that could not justify Israel (Galatians 2:16). When the temple burned, those works ended. A broader reading links "found" to Paul's picture of fire testing each person's work (1 Corinthians 3:13). Either way, the focus is God's judgment of human works, not the burning of rocks.
examples: Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus (4th century) read "will be found" in 2 Peter 3:10.
1 Corinthians 3:13: each person's work will be revealed by fire, and the fire will test it.
questions.other: Most interpreters accept the reading "will be found" but apply it to the final judgment, when the earth and all deeds on it are exposed before God. They see "works" as all human deeds, not specifically the works of the Mosaic law.

questions.q: What promise did Peter mean in "according to his promise we look for new heavens and a new earth" (2 Peter 3:13)?
questions.short: The promise of Isaiah 65:17 and 66:22, the only Old Testament texts with that phrase. The fulfilled reading says Isaiah ties the new heavens and earth to a new Jerusalem and people, so Peter meant the new covenant world.
questions.answer: Peter says believers wait for new heavens and a new earth "according to his promise", in which righteousness lives (2 Peter 3:13). Most agree he points to Isaiah. Isaiah 65:17-18 says God will create new heavens and a new earth, and then explains: he creates Jerusalem as a joy and her people a delight. Isaiah 66:22 says that as the new heavens and earth remain, so will your seed and your name. On the fulfilled reading, Isaiah's new creation is a renewed people of God. That fits Peter's phrase "where righteousness dwells", because righteousness lives in people. Paul says believers in Christ are made "the righteousness of God" (2 Corinthians 5:21). Peter waited for this new world to stand alone after the old was removed.
examples: Isaiah 65:17-18 places "new heavens and new earth" next to "I create Jerusalem a rejoicing".
2 Corinthians 5:17-21: in Christ there is a new creation; we become the righteousness of God in him.
questions.other: Most readers agree the promise is Isaiah 65-66. But they argue Isaiah pictures a renewed physical world and people together, and Peter, after a world-ending fire, expects a renewed cosmos. Gentry, Bauckham and Middleton all read 2 Peter 3:13 as the final new creation.

questions.q: What were the "first heaven and the first earth" that passed away (Revelation 21:1)?
questions.short: On the covenantal reading, the old covenant world: Israel's temple-centred order that began at Sinai, or, on a stronger form, began in Eden. It passed away in AD 70.
questions.answer: Revelation 21:1 says John saw a new heaven and a new earth, for the first heaven and first earth had passed away, and there was no more sea. Isaiah 65:17 says the former things will not be remembered. The parallel is clear. On one covenantal reading, the "first" heaven and earth is the Mosaic covenant world, which Hebrews calls "the first" covenant (Hebrews 8:7, 13; 9:1, 8). On a stronger form, "first" points back to Genesis 1, read as the start of God's covenant people from Adam onward. Either way, John saw the old pass and the new city come. Revelation says its events were "soon" (Revelation 1:1, 3; 22:6, 10), which supports a first-century setting.
examples: Hebrews 9:8: the way into the holy place was not yet open "while the first tabernacle was still standing".
Revelation 22:10: John is told not to seal the book, "for the time is at hand", unlike Daniel 12:4.
questions.other: Most interpreters say the first heaven and earth is the present physical universe, which passes away or is renewed at Christ's return (Revelation 20:11). They see Revelation 20:11-15 (the final judgment) leading straight into chapter 21.

questions.q: Does Scripture speak of any other creation of "the heavens and the earth" besides Genesis 1?
questions.short: One covenantal paper says no, and so identifies the "first heaven and earth" with Genesis 1, read covenantally. Others point to Isaiah 51:16, where God "plants the heavens" at the exodus, as a second covenant creation.
questions.answer: Genesis 1:1 is the first creation of heaven and earth. One covenantal paper argues there is no other such creation in Scripture, so the "first heaven and earth" in Revelation 21:1 must be the Genesis creation, which it reads as a covenant creation of God's people. But other covenantal readers point to Isaiah 51:15-16, where God says he divided the sea and put his words in Zion's mouth "to plant the heavens and found the earth". This places a "creation" at the exodus and Sinai. Deuteronomy 32:6 also says God "made" and "established" Israel. On this view, the first heaven and earth of Revelation 21 is the Sinai covenant world, not Genesis 1.
examples: Isaiah 51:16: God plants the heavens and founds the earth when he says to Zion, "You are my people."
Deuteronomy 32:6: "Is he not your father, who created you, who made you and established you?"
questions.other: Traditional readers hold that Genesis 1 is the one physical creation, and Revelation 21 brings its renewal. They see the exodus language of "creating" Israel as figurative. Hence, they think the first heaven and earth must be the physical one.

questions.q: Is the "new heavens and new earth" of Isaiah 65:17-19 and 66:22 about a covenant people?
questions.short: On the covenantal reading, yes. Isaiah explains the new heavens and earth at once as a new Jerusalem and a joyful people, and promises "your seed and your name" will remain as they do.
questions.answer: Isaiah 65:17 says God creates new heavens and a new earth, and the former things will not be remembered. Verse 18 says: rejoice in what I create, for I create Jerusalem a joy and her people a gladness. Verse 19 says weeping will no longer be heard in her. Isaiah 66:22 says that as the new heavens and new earth remain before God, so will your offspring and your name. On the covenantal reading, the text defines its own terms. The new creation is a city and a people. It stands as long as God's people stand. The setting is covenant: God judges rebels (65:11-15) and blesses his servants. This is the glory of the new covenant, not a new solar system.
examples: Isaiah 65:18: "I create Jerusalem a rejoicing, and her people a joy" (KJV).
Isaiah 66:22 links the lasting of the new heavens and earth with the lasting of Israel's seed and name.
questions.other: Most commentators agree Isaiah focuses on a renewed Jerusalem and people. Many hold that the people and their world are renewed together, as in Isaiah 11:6-9 and 35:1-2. Premillennialists often see a millennial earth in 65:20-25, and the eternal state in Revelation 21.

questions.q: What did Isaiah mean when he said God would slay the scorners and call his servants "by another name" (Isaiah 65:13-15)?
questions.short: God would judge the rebels in Israel and give his faithful servants a new name. The fulfilled reading sees this in the parables of the vineyard and the wedding feast, and in the name "Christians".
questions.answer: Isaiah 65:13-14 contrasts God's servants, who eat, drink and rejoice, with the rebels, who are hungry, thirsty and ashamed. Verse 15 says the rebels will leave their name as a curse, the Lord God will put them to death, and he will call his servants by another name. On the fulfilled reading, Jesus told the same story. In the parable of the vineyard, the owner destroys the wicked tenants and gives the vineyard to others (Matthew 21:41, 43). In the wedding parable, the king burns the murderers' city and invites new guests (Matthew 22:7-10). The new name came too: "the disciples were first called Christians at Antioch" (Acts 11:26).
examples: Acts 11:26 (about AD 40-44): the disciples were first called Christians at Antioch.
Matthew 21:43: the kingdom will be taken from you and given to a people producing its fruits.
questions.other: Others agree Isaiah contrasts the faithful and the faithless within Israel. Many caution against reading Matthew 21:43 as God rejecting the Jewish people; the believing remnant was Jewish (Romans 11:1-5). Some see the "new name" as Revelation 2:17 and 3:12, given at the end.

questions.q: Will the new heavens and new earth be a physical paradise with no death, pain or tears?
questions.short: The covenantal reading says Isaiah 65 cannot be that, because death still happens in it (65:20). It reads the new creation as the new covenant life now, where spiritual death and condemnation are removed.
questions.answer: Many teach that God will remake the universe as a paradise with no death. But Isaiah's new heavens and earth still have death. A person who dies at a hundred is "a child" (Isaiah 65:20). A sinner is still cursed. People build and plant (65:21-22). Isaiah 66:24 even ends with the corpses of rebels outside the city. On the covenantal reading, this cannot describe a world with no death at all. It describes the new covenant age. In Christ there is no condemnation (Romans 8:1). Believers have passed from death to life (John 5:24). The tears and sorrow removed are the guilt and curse of the law. So the new creation is a present spiritual reality, growing in the world.
examples: Isaiah 65:20: "the child shall die an hundred years old" (KJV) — death is still present.
Isaiah 66:24: those who worship look on the corpses of the rebels outside.
questions.other: Premillennialists answer that Isaiah 65:20-25 describes the millennium, and Revelation 21 the eternal state. Amillennialists say Isaiah uses long life as a picture of perfect blessing, in the language his hearers knew. Both hold that Revelation 21:4 promises an end of physical death (1 Corinthians 15:26).

questions.q: What do the long lives, houses and vineyards of Isaiah 65:20-22 mean?
questions.short: On the covenantal reading, they are pictures of new covenant blessing: long life pictures eternal life, and eating the fruit of the vine pictures sharing in Christ, the true vine.
questions.answer: Isaiah 65:20 says there will be no infant who lives only a few days, nor an old man who does not fill his days. Verses 21-22 say people will build houses and live in them, plant vineyards and eat their fruit, and their days will be like the days of a tree. Under the old covenant's curses, others ate what Israel planted (Deuteronomy 28:30). In the new order, the curse is reversed. On the covenantal reading, long life stands for the eternal life found in Christ. The vineyard points to Jesus, the true vine (John 15:1-5). "The days of a tree" recalls the tree of life (Revelation 22:2). These are covenant blessings in picture language.
examples: Deuteronomy 28:30: a curse of the old covenant — you will plant a vineyard and not use its fruit.
John 15:5: "I am the vine, you are the branches."
questions.other: Premillennialists read these as literal conditions in Christ's thousand-year reign on earth. Many amillennialists and others read them as poetic pictures of the final new creation, using the best blessings an Israelite could imagine. Few take them as a description of the present church age.

questions.q: What do the wolf and lamb feeding together mean (Isaiah 65:25)?
questions.short: On the covenantal reading, they picture former enemies, such as Jews and Gentiles, reconciled in Christ. "Dust shall be the serpent's food" recalls the curse on the serpent in Eden.
questions.answer: Isaiah 65:25 says the wolf and the lamb will feed together, the lion will eat straw like the ox, dust will be the serpent's food, and they will not hurt or destroy in all God's holy mountain. Isaiah 11:6-9 has a similar picture, and ends with the earth full of the knowledge of the Lord. On the covenantal reading, these animals stand for peoples. Jews and Gentiles were enemies, but Christ "made both one" and broke down the wall between them (Ephesians 2:14-16). The serpent eating dust recalls Genesis 3:14. The curse falls on the deceiver, while God's people are safe. The "holy mountain" is Zion, the church (Hebrews 12:22).
examples: Ephesians 2:14-16: Christ made Jew and Gentile one new man, ending the hostility.
Acts 10:11-15: Peter's vision of clean and unclean animals pictured Gentiles accepted by God.
questions.other: Many interpreters read the animals literally, as real peace in a renewed creation or in the millennium (Romans 8:21). Others accept symbolism but see it as peace in the whole new creation, not only in the church. Most agree the serpent line recalls Genesis 3.

questions.q: Was "new heavens and new earth" familiar language to first-century Jews?
questions.short: Yes. It came from Isaiah, and Jewish writings of the time also used it. The covenantal reading says that New Testament writers expected readers to hear it as Isaiah meant it.
questions.answer: Isaiah 65:17 and 66:22 gave the phrase. Jewish works before and around Jesus' time echoed it. 1 Enoch 91:16 speaks of the first heaven passing and a new heaven appearing. The Bible itself also uses the idea of a new world or new age for covenant change: Jesus speaks of "the regeneration" (Matthew 19:28), and Paul of a "new creation" (2 Corinthians 5:17; Galatians 6:15). On the covenantal reading, the apostles did not invent new terms. They used words their hearers knew from the Old Testament, where "heaven and earth" could describe God's people. So to understand Revelation 21 and 2 Peter 3, readers must first ask how Isaiah used the phrase.
examples: Matthew 19:28: "in the regeneration (palingenesia), when the Son of Man sits on his glorious throne".
Galatians 6:15: what counts is "a new creation", not circumcision or uncircumcision.
questions.other: Others agree the language was familiar, but note that Jewish texts such as 1 Enoch and 4 Ezra often expected a real renewal of the world. They argue that first-century hearers would therefore expect a cosmic renewal, with covenant meaning included.

questions.q: How can "no more death, mourning, crying or pain" (Revelation 21:3-4) be true now?
questions.short: On the covenantal reading, it describes life in the new covenant, where God dwells with his people and the curse of sin and the law's condemnation are gone, because "the former things have passed".
questions.answer: Revelation 21:3 says God's tabernacle is with people; he will dwell with them, and they will be his people. Verse 4 says he will wipe away every tear, and there will be no more death, sorrow, crying or pain, for the former things have passed away. On the covenantal reading, the "former things" are the old covenant order, with its law of sin and death (Romans 8:2). Under it, people lived in guilt and fear of death (Hebrews 2:15). In Christ, God dwells in his people (2 Corinthians 6:16). Death has lost its sting (1 Corinthians 15:55-57). The tears wiped away are the sorrow of separation from God. Believers still die bodily, but they do not face the "second death" (Revelation 21:8).
examples: Hebrews 2:14-15: Christ freed those who lived all their lives in slavery to the fear of death.
2 Corinthians 6:16: "I will dwell in them and walk among them" — Paul applies the promise to the church now.
questions.other: Most Christians read Revelation 21:4 as the future state after the resurrection, when physical death itself is destroyed (1 Corinthians 15:26, 54). They note that believers still mourn and die today, so they see the promise as future, with a foretaste now.

questions.q: What does "Behold, I make all things new" mean (Revelation 21:5-7)?
questions.short: On the covenantal reading, Christ's new covenant work: a new people, new birth and new life. "It is done" marks the full arrival of that new order once the old had passed.
questions.answer: Revelation 21:5 says the One on the throne declares, "I make all things new." Verse 6 says, "It is done," and he gives the water of life freely to the thirsty. Verse 7 says the one who overcomes will inherit all things and be God's son. Paul uses the same idea: if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation; the old has passed away, the new has come (2 Corinthians 5:17). The verb in Revelation 21:5 is present: "I am making". On the covenantal reading, this is God's ongoing work in Christ. The water of life is offered now: "let the one who is thirsty come" (Revelation 22:17).
examples: 2 Corinthians 5:17: "the old things passed away; behold, new things have come."
Revelation 22:17: the Spirit and the bride say "Come", and the water of life is free.
questions.other: Most interpreters agree the new creation begins in believers now, but say "all things new" points to the whole creation made new at the end (Romans 8:21; Acts 3:21). They see 2 Corinthians 5:17 as the first stage of a cosmic renewal.

questions.q: How can nations and kings bring their glory into the city if the new creation is after the end of history (Revelation 21:24-26)?
questions.short: The covenantal reading says this fits the present gospel age: the nations walk in the city's light and their kings bring their glory into the church, while the gates stay open.
questions.answer: Revelation 21:24 says the nations will walk by its light, and the kings of the earth will bring their glory into it. Verse 25 says its gates will never be shut. Verse 27 says nothing unclean will enter. Revelation 22:2 says the leaves of the tree are for the healing of the nations. On the covenantal reading, these details suit the present. There are still nations to heal and kings to bring gifts. There are still unclean people outside (22:15). Isaiah 60:3-11, which John is quoting, pictures nations coming to Zion's light. That is the gospel going out. One covenantal paper sees the "nations" as Gentile believers and the "kings" as Jewish believers, though the text does not split them this way.
examples: Isaiah 60:3, 11: nations come to your light; your gates stay open day and night.
Revelation 22:15: outside are dogs, sorcerers and liars — evil still exists outside the city.
questions.other: Futurist and amillennial readers say the nations and kings are the redeemed peoples bringing their honour into the eternal city. They read "outside" in 22:15 as the lake of fire, and the healing leaves as lasting life, not ongoing evangelism.

questions.q: Is the new Jerusalem a physical city?
questions.short: On the covenantal reading, no. Its gates bear the twelve tribes, its foundations the twelve apostles, and it is shaped like the Most Holy Place. It is the people of God, the bride.
questions.answer: Revelation 21:12-14 gives the city twelve gates with the names of Israel's twelve tribes, and twelve foundations with the names of the twelve apostles. Its length, width and height are equal, 12,000 stadia, about 2,200 km (21:16). It is a cube, like the Most Holy Place in Solomon's temple (1 Kings 6:20). On the covenantal reading, this is not a building plan. It shows God's people as his dwelling. Paul says believers are built on the foundation of apostles and prophets, with Christ as cornerstone (Ephesians 2:20). Hebrews says believers "have come" to the heavenly Jerusalem (Hebrews 12:22). Paul calls "the Jerusalem above" our mother (Galatians 4:26).
examples: 1 Kings 6:20: the inner sanctuary was 20 cubits long, wide and high — a cube.
Ephesians 2:20-22: the church is built on the apostles and prophets into a holy temple.
questions.other: Many futurists read the city as a real place where the saints will live, with symbolic features. Others, such as Robert Gundry, say the city is the people, but the people live in a renewed physical world. Most agree its cube shape points to the Most Holy Place.

questions.q: What does it mean that the angel promised to show "the bride" and showed a city (Revelation 21:9-10)?
questions.short: The text treats the bride and the city as one. The covenantal reading concludes that the new Jerusalem, and so the new heavens and earth, are the church, the people married to Christ.
questions.answer: In Revelation 21:9 an angel says to John, "Come, I will show you the bride, the wife of the Lamb." In verse 10 he shows John the holy city Jerusalem coming down from God. The bride is the city. Revelation 19:7-8 says the bride's fine linen is the righteous acts of the saints, so the bride is a people. Paul pictures the church as Christ's bride (Ephesians 5:25-27; 2 Corinthians 11:2). On the covenantal reading, if the new Jerusalem is the bride, and the bride is the church, then the "new heaven and new earth" John saw with the city is the new covenant people and their life with God. That also shows that "first heaven and earth" was a people and their order.
examples: Revelation 19:8: the fine linen "is the righteousness of saints" (KJV).
Revelation 17-18 shows the other city, Babylon the harlot, also a city that is a woman.
questions.other: Many readers agree the city pictures the people. But they say a city also implies a place, and the new earth is where the bride lives. They think the new heaven and earth in 21:1 is the setting, and the city in 21:2 is the people within it.

questions.q: If the Bible is about God redeeming his people, how does recreating a physical universe fit in?
questions.short: The covenantal reading says it fits poorly. Redemption is about people, so the new heavens and earth are best read as a redeemed people. Others say redeemed people need a renewed world, as bodies need resurrection.
questions.answer: Asked to sum up the Bible in one phrase, many would say "God and the redemption of his people". The covenantal reading asks: how does a remade solar system serve that story? Stars do not sin and are not saved. On this reading, the creation and new creation language is about God making a people for himself. Israel was formed and judged in "heaven and earth" language. The church is the new heaven and earth, where God dwells with his redeemed. Jesus said his kingdom does not come with observable signs, but is "among you" (Luke 17:20-21). The focus is relationship with God through covenant, not the physics of the universe.
examples: Titus 2:14: Christ gave himself to redeem us and purify a people for his own possession.
Luke 17:20-21: the kingdom does not come with signs to be watched; it is in your midst.
questions.other: Many reply that redemption includes the body. Jesus rose with a physical body (Luke 24:39), and believers will too (Romans 8:23). Since bodies need a world, God renews creation (Romans 8:21; Colossians 1:20). Writers such as N. T. Wright and J. Richard Middleton argue the Bible's story ends with heaven and earth joined, not with escape from matter.

questions.q: Did older Christian scholars read "the passing of heaven and earth" as the end of the Jewish order?
questions.short: Yes, some did. John Lightfoot, John Owen and John Brown, all respected Reformed scholars, applied certain "heaven and earth" texts to the fall of Jerusalem and the Mosaic order.
questions.answer: John Lightfoot (1602-1675), a Hebrew scholar at the Westminster Assembly, wrote that "heaven and earth passing" in Matthew 24:35 meant the destruction of Jerusalem and the Jewish state, as if the whole world-frame were dissolved. John Owen (1616-1683) preached that 2 Peter 3:5-7 described the desolation of the Jewish church and state, not the last judgment. John Brown of Edinburgh (1784-1858), on Matthew 5:18, said that a reader familiar with the Old Testament knows the end of the Mosaic economy is spoken of as old heavens and earth removed. On the fulfilled reading, this shows the covenantal reading is not new. Careful scholars long before modern debates saw it.
examples: Lightfoot's Horae Hebraicae et Talmudicae (1658-1674) is still used for Jewish background to the Gospels.
Owen's sermon "Providential Changes, an Argument for Universal Holiness" applies 2 Peter 3 to the Jewish state.
questions.other: Others note that these same scholars still believed in a future bodily return, resurrection and final judgment. Owen and Lightfoot did not apply every "new heavens" text to AD 70. Most historic theologians, including Calvin, read 2 Peter 3 and Revelation 21 as the final renewal.

questions.q: Is "if the plain sense makes good sense, seek no other sense" a safe rule for reading "heaven and earth"?
questions.short: The covenantal reading says it is not, if "plain" means plain to a modern reader. Readers must ask what the words meant to the first hearers, who knew prophetic imagery.
questions.answer: David L. Cooper, a dispensational teacher, made famous the rule: when the plain sense makes common sense, seek no other sense. The covenantal reading says this rule can mislead. A modern reader sees "heaven and earth" and thinks of galaxies and the planet from space. A first-century Jew had Isaiah's oracles, the temple, and the Song of Moses in mind. The "plain sense" for him could be covenantal. Jesus' own hearers often missed his figures: they thought "destroy this temple" meant the building (John 2:19-21). Nicodemus took "born again" literally (John 3:4). On the fulfilled reading, the safe rule is to compare Scripture with Scripture and let the Bible's own usage decide.
examples: John 2:19-21: the hearers took "this temple" as Herod's building; Jesus meant his body.
Isaiah 13:10 shows that the "plain sense" for a prophet could be a collapsing sky meaning a fallen empire.
questions.other: Dispensationalists reply that a literal method means the normal sense in context, including figures of speech. They agree that prophecy uses images, but say figures must be shown by the text. They warn that without this rule, almost any text can be spiritualised.

questions.q: Is the Bible one story from Genesis to Revelation, with the New Testament picking up where Malachi ended?
questions.short: Yes, all readings agree. Malachi ends with Elijah coming before the day of the Lord, and the Gospels open with John the Baptist as that Elijah. So the New Testament uses Old Testament language.
questions.answer: Malachi 4:5-6 promises Elijah before the great and dreadful day of the Lord, lest God strike the land with a curse. After about 400 years without a prophet, Mark 1:2-3 opens with "as it is written in the prophets" and introduces John. Jesus said John was the Elijah who was to come (Matthew 11:13-14). On the fulfilled reading, this matters for heaven and earth. If John is Elijah, then the "great and dreadful day" came soon after him, in that generation. And if the Bible is one story, the New Testament's "heaven and earth" language should be read in the light of the Old Testament, where it often described God's covenant people.
examples: Malachi 4:5: Elijah comes before the great and dreadful day; Matthew 11:14: "this is Elijah who was to come."
Luke 1:17: John goes "in the spirit and power of Elijah" to prepare a people.
questions.other: All Christian traditions affirm the unity of Scripture. Futurists add that Elijah may come again before the final day (Revelation 11:3-6). Others agree John fulfilled Malachi, but see the great day as including both AD 70 and the last judgment.

questions.q: What is our authority for this question: church history, the creeds, or Scripture?
questions.short: All Protestant views say Scripture is the final authority. The covenantal reading admits it differs from many creeds and traditions here, but asks readers to judge by Scripture alone.
questions.answer: The covenantal reading openly says it goes against much church history, the creeds and tradition. It then asks: what is our authority? The Reformers taught that Scripture is the highest judge in all questions of faith. The Westminster Confession says the supreme judge is the Holy Spirit speaking in Scripture (1.10). The Bereans tested even Paul's words by the Scriptures (Acts 17:11). On this reading, the creeds are valuable guides, but they can be corrected by the Bible. If Scripture uses "heaven and earth" as covenant language, then believers should follow Scripture even when it changes a long-held view. The writer adds a humble note: he does not claim to have all the answers.
examples: Acts 17:11: the Bereans examined the Scriptures daily to see if these things were so.
Westminster Confession 1.10: the supreme judge of all controversies is the Holy Spirit speaking in Scripture.
questions.other: Others agree Scripture is supreme but say the creeds hold the church's shared reading of it. The Nicene Creed confesses "the resurrection of the dead and the life of the world to come". They argue that when a reading departs from all historic Christian teaching, the burden of proof is very high.

questions.q: What kind of book is the Bible: a science book about the universe, or a covenant book about God and people?
questions.short: The covenantal reading says it is mainly a book of covenant, showing how God relates to mankind. It uses heaven and earth as images of that relationship, without lessening the glory of the physical creation.
questions.answer: The covenantal reading asks: what was God's main purpose in giving Scripture? Is it a science book written to prove that God made the universe? Or is it mainly a covenant book that shows how God relates to his people? It concludes the second. The Bible's own summary of its purpose is about salvation: the Scriptures make one "wise unto salvation" through faith in Christ (2 Timothy 3:15). John wrote "that you may believe" (John 20:31). On this reading, God uses heaven and earth as pictures for his covenant with his people. This does not deny the physical creation's glory. It points to a greater glory: his covenant with mankind and his new creation in Christ.
examples: 2 Timothy 3:15: the Scriptures make you "wise unto salvation through faith which is in Christ Jesus" (KJV).
John 20:31: "these are written, that ye might believe that Jesus is the Christ" (KJV).
questions.other: Others agree the Bible is not a science textbook and is centred on covenant. But they say covenant includes creation: God made a covenant with every living creature (Genesis 9:10) and with day and night (Jeremiah 33:25). They think a covenant reading should embrace, not replace, the physical world.

tabernacle.name: The outer court
tabernacle.represents: The land and the sea: the visible, inhabited world, open to all.
tabernacle.text: Josephus says Moses divided the tabernacle into three parts. He gave two to the priests as common, open places, and he says they stand for the land and the sea, which all people can reach (Antiquities 3.7.7, sections 181-182). Strictly, Josephus is probably speaking of the three portions of the tent itself (Antiquities 3.6.4 splits it into 20 cubits and 10 cubits). Later readers, ancient and modern, applied the same idea to the outer court. In Solomon's temple the great bronze basin was called "the sea" (1 Kings 7:23-26). In Ezekiel's temple the base of the altar is, in Hebrew, the "bosom of the earth" (Ezekiel 43:14). Scholars such as G. K. Beale and Jon Levenson take the court as the picture of the earth and sea where humanity lives.

tabernacle.name: The holy place
tabernacle.represents: The visible heavens: sun, moon and stars, the lights God set in the sky.
tabernacle.text: In the holy place stood the lampstand with seven lamps, the table with twelve loaves and the altar of incense. Josephus says the seven lamps stand for the seven "planets" known in his day, and the twelve loaves for the circle of the zodiac and the twelve months (Jewish War 5.5.5, sections 216-218; compare Antiquities 3.7.7). The curtain at the entrance to Herod's temple was embroidered with a panorama of the heavens, in four colours that stood for the elements (Jewish War 5.5.4, sections 212-214). Philo of Alexandria made similar links (Life of Moses 2.102-105). On this reading, the priests served in a model of the sky, with the lamps as its lights (Genesis 1:14-16 uses "lights" for sun and moon, the same word used of the lampstand's light in Exodus 35:14).

tabernacle.name: The most holy place
tabernacle.represents: The highest heaven, God's own dwelling and throne, which no human can reach.
tabernacle.text: Josephus says Moses set apart the third part for God, "because heaven is inaccessible to men" (Antiquities 3.7.7, section 181). In Herod's temple this inner room held nothing at all (Jewish War 5.5.5, section 219). Only the high priest entered, once a year, with blood (Leviticus 16:2, 34). The ark with its cherubim was God's footstool and throne (1 Chronicles 28:2; Psalms 99:1). Hebrews says Christ entered "not into holy places made with hands" but "into heaven itself" (Hebrews 9:24, KJV), so the inner room was a copy of the true heaven. When the curtain tore at Jesus' death (Matthew 27:51), the way into God's presence was opened (Hebrews 10:19-20). In Revelation 21:16 the new Jerusalem is a perfect cube, like the most holy place (1 Kings 6:20).

echoes.echoPhrase: I beheld the earth, and, lo, it was without form, and void
echoes.note: This exact pair of Hebrew words appears only here and in Genesis 1:2. Jeremiah sees Judah's coming ruin by Babylon (586 BC) as creation run backwards: no light, no people, no birds, fruitful land turned to wilderness (Jeremiah 4:23-26). Yet God adds, "I will not make a full end" (Jeremiah 4:27). All readers agree this is judgment on the land and people, told in creation words. Isaiah 34:11 also uses tohu and bohu for Edom's ruin.

echoes.genesisPhrase: the Spirit of God moved (hovered) upon the face of the waters
echoes.echoPhrase: as an eagle stirreth up her nest, fluttereth over her young
echoes.note: The rare verb rachaph (to hover) is used in Genesis 1:2 and Deuteronomy 32:11. One verse earlier God finds Israel in a "waste howling wilderness" (Deuteronomy 32:10), where "waste" is tohu, the word of Genesis 1:2. So Moses tells Israel's rescue as a new creation: God hovers over a formless place and brings out a people. Jesus uses a similar bird picture over Jerusalem just before he announces its desolation (Matthew 23:37-38).

echoes.genesisPhrase: the Spirit (ruach) of God moved upon the face of the waters
echoes.echoPhrase: God made a wind (ruach) to pass over the earth, and the waters asswaged
echoes.note: After the flood, God sends a ruach over the waters, dry land appears and Noah is told to "be fruitful and multiply" (Genesis 9:1), as Adam was. The flood is told as an un-creation and a new start. 2 Peter 3:6 calls it the end of "the world that then was".

echoes.theme: Dividing the waters, dry land appearing
echoes.echoPhrase: the LORD caused the sea to go back by a strong east wind ... and made the sea dry land
echoes.note: At the Red Sea, a wind divides the waters and dry ground appears, as on day three. Israel walks through as a new people. Isaiah 51:9-10 ties the sea crossing to God's victory over the chaos waters and then speaks of God planting the heavens and founding the earth for Zion (Isaiah 51:16).

echoes.genesisPhrase: God divided the light from the darkness
echoes.echoPhrase: all the children of Israel had light in their dwellings
echoes.note: In the ninth plague Egypt is plunged back into darkness while Israel has light. God again "divides" light from darkness, now between peoples. The prophets use the same pattern: darkness for judgment (Amos 8:9) and light rising on God's people (Isaiah 60:1-2).

echoes.genesisPhrase: Be fruitful, and multiply, and replenish the earth
echoes.echoPhrase: the children of Israel were fruitful, and increased abundantly, and multiplied ... and the land was filled
echoes.note: Exodus 1:7 uses the words of the creation blessing for Israel in Egypt. The nation is presented as the carrier of Adam's calling. The promise to Abraham of seed like stars and dust (Genesis 22:17) points the same way.

echoes.genesisPhrase: he rested on the seventh day from all his work
echoes.echoPhrase: There remaineth therefore a rest to the people of God
echoes.note: God's rest after creation becomes Israel's Sabbath (Exodus 20:11), then rest in the land (Joshua 21:44), then the temple as God's resting place (Psalms 132:13-14). Hebrews says a deeper rest remains, entered by faith in Christ. Readers differ on whether that rest is mainly present, future, or both.

echoes.genesisPhrase: the heavens and the earth were finished ... God ended his work
echoes.note: The tabernacle story closes with words that recall the end of creation: the work is finished, Moses sees it and blesses (Exodus 39:43; compare Genesis 1:31; 2:3). Many scholars see the tabernacle as a small creation. This is one basis for reading the sanctuary as a "heaven and earth".

echoes.genesisPhrase: breathed into his nostrils the breath of life
echoes.echoPhrase: Come from the four winds, O breath, and breathe upon these slain
echoes.note: Ezekiel sees exiled Israel as dry bones. God breathes on them, as on Adam, and they live: the nation is re-created (Ezekiel 37:11-14). Jesus breathes on the disciples and says "Receive the Holy Spirit" (John 20:22), a new-creation act on the first day of the week.

echoes.genesisPhrase: the LORD God planted a garden eastward in Eden
echoes.echoPhrase: he will make her wilderness like Eden, and her desert like the garden of the LORD
echoes.note: Return from exile is pictured as Eden regained (also Ezekiel 36:35). Revelation 22:1-2 brings back the river and the tree of life inside the holy city. Readers differ on whether the garden is fulfilled in the church, in a renewed earth, or in both.

echoes.genesisPhrase: Let there be light: and there was light
echoes.echoPhrase: God, who commanded the light to shine out of darkness, hath shined in our hearts
echoes.note: Paul says the God who spoke light at creation has now spoken light into believers' hearts through the face of Christ. Conversion is a creation act. This is a clear case where the New Testament uses Genesis 1 for a spiritual reality without denying that Genesis 1 also happened.

echoes.echoPhrase: if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature (new creation)
echoes.note: Paul's phrase can be read as "there is a new creation". The old things have passed away and new things have come. Galatians 6:15 says what counts is "a new creation". The covenantal reading sees this as the new heavens and earth already present. The already/not-yet reading agrees it has begun and expects its completion at the resurrection (Romans 8:21-23).

atlas.phrase: In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth
atlas.covenantal: Most covenant readers accept a real creation here, but note that the Bible opens and closes with 'heaven and earth', so the phrase frames the whole story of God and his people. A minority reads Genesis 1 itself as the forming of a covenant people.
atlas.physical: God made the whole universe from nothing. 'Heaven and earth' is a Hebrew way of saying 'everything', as in Exodus 20:11 and Nehemiah 9:6.

atlas.phrase: Thus the heavens and the earth were finished
atlas.covenantal: 'Host' (tsaba) is often an army word, so this reading sees a hint of an ordered people. The finished 'heavens and earth' is also the pattern later used for the tabernacle, which Moses 'finished' in Exodus 40:33.
atlas.physical: The six days are complete and the created order is whole. The 'host' are the stars and every creature that fills sky and land.

atlas.phrase: the generations of the heavens and of the earth
atlas.covenantal: 'Generations' (toledot) elsewhere introduces family lines (Genesis 5:1; 25:19; 37:2). This reading says the heavens and earth here open the story of a human family, Adam and his line.
atlas.physical: The toledot formula marks a new section. Here it tells what came from the created world, especially the making of man in Genesis 2.

atlas.phrase: make thy seed as the dust of the earth
atlas.covenantal: God pictures Abraham's family as 'earth'. This is the first clue that earth language can stand for a people in covenant with God.
atlas.physical: This is a simile about number only. Abraham's offspring will be beyond counting, like grains of dust; the earth itself is not a symbol here.

atlas.phrase: Look now toward heaven, and tell the stars
atlas.covenantal: The stars become a picture of Abraham's seed. Together with 'dust of the earth' (13:16), the covenant family is both 'heaven' and 'earth'.
atlas.physical: Abraham looks at the real night sky. The comparison promises a vast family; it does not turn the stars into people.

atlas.phrase: multiply thy seed as the stars of the heaven
atlas.covenantal: Stars of heaven and sand of the shore together describe one covenant family. The oath binds heaven and earth images to Abraham's seed and its blessing to the nations.
atlas.physical: Two pictures of a countless number: stars above and sand below. The promise is about growth, not about the meaning of the cosmos.

atlas.phrase: the sun and the moon and the eleven stars
atlas.covenantal: Jacob reads the dream at once: sun, moon and stars are his household (37:10). Heavenly lights stand for the covenant family and its rulers, a key for Revelation 12:1.
atlas.physical: This is a dream with its own interpretation inside the text. It shows that dreams and visions may use stars as symbols, not that ordinary 'heaven and earth' texts are symbols.

atlas.phrase: I call heaven and earth to witness against you
atlas.covenantal: In ancient treaties the gods were called as witnesses. Moses calls heaven and earth instead, the lasting parties around the covenant, and the warning is loss of the land.
atlas.physical: The created world is personified as a lasting witness. It outlives each generation, so it can 'testify' that the terms were given.

atlas.phrase: I call heaven and earth to record this day
atlas.covenantal: Life and death, blessing and curse are set before Israel with heaven and earth as witnesses. The phrase belongs to the language of covenant law.
atlas.physical: Moses appeals to the fixed created order as a solemn witness. The poetry does not deny that he means the real sky and land.

atlas.phrase: call heaven and earth to record against them
atlas.covenantal: The elders and officers gather, and heaven and earth are called to hear. This reading notes that the audience is Israel's leaders, and the song that follows calls Israel itself heaven and earth.
atlas.physical: Heaven and earth witness against the people, as in 4:26. A witness is set apart from the accused, so heaven and earth are not the people here.

atlas.phrase: Give ear, O ye heavens ... and hear, O earth
atlas.covenantal: The Song of Moses then uses Genesis 1 words for Israel's birth: 'waste' (tohu, 32:10) and 'flutters' over its young (rachaph, 32:11; Genesis 1:2). Israel is a covenant creation.
atlas.physical: This is a formal call to witnesses at the start of a covenant lawsuit song. The Genesis echoes show God's care, not that Israel is the cosmos.

atlas.phrase: The heaven shall reveal his iniquity
atlas.covenantal: Sky and dirt cannot literally testify. The verse shows that heaven and earth language can describe moral and covenant realities, here God's judgment on the wicked.
