atlas.physical: Zophar uses poetry: heaven (God above) exposes the sinner and the earth (his surroundings) turns against him. It is personification, not a code for a nation.

atlas.phrase: The heavens declare the glory of God
atlas.covenantal: The heavens 'speak' and their 'line' goes to all the earth; Paul applies 19:4 to the preaching of the gospel (Romans 10:18). The heavens can picture God's messengers.
atlas.physical: Verses 1-6 praise God's glory in the sky and the sun, then verses 7-14 praise his law. Paul uses the wording, but the psalm itself speaks of creation's silent witness.

atlas.phrase: call to the heavens from above, and to the earth
atlas.covenantal: God summons heaven and earth 'that he may judge his people'. The court scene concerns covenant members who made a covenant by sacrifice (50:5).
atlas.physical: Creation is called as witness to a trial, like Deuteronomy 32:1. The judged are the people, not the heavens and earth.

atlas.phrase: Let the heaven and earth praise him
atlas.covenantal: The praise is linked to God saving Zion and building Judah's cities (69:35). Heaven and earth rejoice because the covenant people are restored.
atlas.physical: All creation, 'the seas, and every thing that moveth', is called to praise. It is the normal biblical summons of the whole cosmos.

atlas.phrase: built his sanctuary like high palaces, like the earth
atlas.covenantal: God built the sanctuary like the heights and like the earth he founded. The temple was a small heaven and earth, and Josephus (Antiquities 3.7.7) gives the tabernacle a cosmic meaning.
atlas.physical: The verse compares the temple's stability to the stability of the earth 'for ever'. It actually supports the lasting physical earth.

atlas.phrase: Let the heavens rejoice, and let the earth be glad
atlas.covenantal: Heaven and earth rejoice because the LORD 'cometh to judge the earth' (96:13) and his glory is told among the nations (96:3, 10). The covenant reading links this to the gospel going to the Gentiles.
atlas.physical: Sky, sea, fields and trees (96:11-12) are called to rejoice at God's coming reign. It is the real creation personified in praise.

atlas.phrase: the heavens ... shall perish, but thou shalt endure
atlas.covenantal: The psalm is about rebuilding Zion (102:13-16). Like a garment changed, one covenant order gives way to another. Hebrews 1:10-12 applies it to the Son who outlasts the old order.
atlas.physical: The created heavens are old and will wear out, but God is unchanging. The garment image suggests change and renewal, not mere annihilation.

atlas.phrase: the earth, that it should not be removed for ever
atlas.covenantal: If the planet is never removed, then texts where heaven and earth 'pass away' within one generation must mean something other than the planet.
atlas.physical: The physical earth is stable by God's decree. Many see this as compatible with a renewed earth: it is changed, not abolished.

atlas.phrase: for ever, O LORD, thy word is settled in heaven
atlas.covenantal: God's faithfulness is compared to the earth that 'abideth'. The created order is the guarantee of covenant promises, so it cannot be the thing that passes in AD 70.
atlas.physical: The heavens and earth continue by God's ordinances (119:91). Both views agree this is the physical world serving God.

atlas.phrase: but the earth abideth for ever
atlas.covenantal: Generations pass but the earth remains. So when Jesus says heaven and earth will pass within a generation, he must mean a covenant world, not the planet.
atlas.physical: 'For ever' (olam) can mean 'for a very long age'. The Preacher contrasts short human life with the lasting earth; it does not rule out a final renewal.

atlas.phrase: Hear, O heavens, and give ear, O earth
atlas.covenantal: Isaiah opens with Moses' words (Deuteronomy 32:1). In 1:10 the leaders are 'rulers of Sodom'; this reading sees heaven and earth as Israel's rulers and people addressed in covenant lawsuit.
atlas.physical: Heaven and earth are called as witnesses against rebel children, as in Deuteronomy. The children are the people; the witnesses are creation.

atlas.phrase: the stars of heaven ... shall not give their light
atlas.covenantal: This is an oracle against Babylon (13:1), fulfilled when the Medes took it in 539 BC (13:17). Darkened lights mean the fall of a kingdom, the same language Jesus uses in Matthew 24:29.
atlas.physical: Most agree the oracle concerns Babylon, though some see a final 'day of the LORD' in it as well. The cosmic images may point beyond Babylon to the end.

atlas.phrase: the heavens shall be rolled together as a scroll
atlas.covenantal: The target is Edom (34:5-6). Its heavens are 'dissolved' though Edom's land still existed afterward, so the language describes a nation's end, not the cosmos.
atlas.physical: Edom is the immediate case, but Revelation 6:14 reuses the image for the final judgment. Local judgment can preview universal judgment.

atlas.phrase: Sing, O ye heavens; for the LORD hath done it
atlas.covenantal: Heaven and earth sing because 'the LORD hath redeemed Jacob'. Creation language celebrates the remaking of the covenant people after exile.
atlas.physical: All creation, including mountains and trees, is called to praise God's redeeming work. It is joyful personification of the real world.

atlas.phrase: Sing, O heavens; and be joyful, O earth
atlas.covenantal: Heaven and earth rejoice because God comforts his people. Paul cites 49:8 as 'now' (2 Corinthians 6:2) and John echoes 49:10 in Revelation 7:16-17, placing this joy in the gospel age.
atlas.physical: The same poetic summons as 44:23. The New Testament fulfilment in the church does not turn the sky and land into the church.

atlas.phrase: the heavens shall vanish away like smoke
atlas.covenantal: Set beside 51:16, where God plants heavens to say to Zion 'Thou art my people', this reading sees an old order passing while God's salvation stays.
atlas.physical: Even the solid universe is temporary compared with God's salvation, which 'shall be for ever'. The contrast is between creation and the Creator's faithfulness.

atlas.phrase: plant the heavens ... say unto Zion, Thou art my people
atlas.covenantal: God planting heavens and laying earth's foundations is tied to making Zion his people at the exodus (51:9-11). Forming a nation is pictured as creating a world.
atlas.physical: God who made the cosmos is able to protect Zion. The creation clause describes his power, and the purpose clause his care for the people.

atlas.phrase: I create new heavens and a new earth
atlas.covenantal: The context includes death at a hundred years, building and planting, and judgment on rebels (65:12-20). These fit a new covenant order in history, not a world without death.
atlas.physical: This is the promise behind 2 Peter 3:13 and Revelation 21:1. Isaiah uses earthly pictures for a new world; some see stages: begun now, completed at the end.

atlas.phrase: the new heavens and the new earth ... shall remain
atlas.covenantal: The new order lasts like the seed and name of God's people, and worship goes on 'from one new moon to another' (66:23). It describes the ongoing gospel age.
atlas.physical: The permanence of the new creation guarantees the permanence of God's people. Many apply it to the final age after the resurrection.

atlas.phrase: the earth ... was without form, and void
atlas.covenantal: Jeremiah uses tohu wabohu of Genesis 1:2 for Judah's ruin by Babylon in 586 BC. The covenant world is 'uncreated', yet God will not make 'a full end' (4:27).
atlas.physical: A poetic picture of a land so ravaged it looks like creation undone. It shows that creation language can describe judgment on a land.

atlas.phrase: If those ordinances depart from before me
atlas.covenantal: The new covenant (31:31-34) is as sure as sun, moon and stars. The fixed sky is a guarantee, so the 'heaven and earth' that passed must be another order.
atlas.physical: God points to the real, regular heavens to assure Israel. The text treats sun and moon as physical, lasting signs.

atlas.phrase: If ye can break my covenant of the day
atlas.covenantal: Day and night form a 'covenant'. The promise to David's son is as firm as creation; it is fulfilled in Christ's reign (Luke 1:32-33).
atlas.physical: God's covenant with creation (Genesis 8:22) is the measuring rod for his covenant with David. The created order is literal here.

atlas.phrase: cover the heaven, and make the stars thereof dark
atlas.covenantal: This is a lament over Pharaoh and Egypt (32:2), fulfilled when Babylon struck Egypt (32:11). Cosmic darkness means a ruler's fall.
atlas.physical: Most agree this describes Egypt's defeat in vivid poetry. Some add that such local 'days' anticipate the final day of the LORD.

atlas.phrase: I will hear the heavens ... they shall hear the earth
atlas.covenantal: In the renewed marriage covenant (2:18-23), heaven answers earth and earth answers Jezreel. Paul applies 2:23 to Jews and Gentiles called in Christ (Romans 9:25-26).
atlas.physical: A chain of blessing: God sends rain from the sky, the land produces grain and wine, and the people are fed. It is a promise of real fruitfulness.

atlas.phrase: wonders in the heavens and in the earth
atlas.covenantal: Peter says 'this is that' at Pentecost (Acts 2:16-20). The signs led up to the 'great and terrible day' that came on Jerusalem within that generation.
atlas.physical: Peter cites the whole text, but some see the cosmic signs as still future, before Christ's return. Others take the darkening at the cross (Luke 23:44-45) as part.

atlas.phrase: I will shake the heavens, and the earth
atlas.covenantal: The shaking is tied to the temple and 'the desire of all nations' (2:7). Hebrews 12:26-28 says it removes what can be shaken, the old order, so an unshakable kingdom remains.
atlas.physical: God's shaking points to his final intervention in history. Hebrews links it to the kingdom, and many take its last stage as the end of the age.

atlas.phrase: Till heaven and earth pass, one jot or one tittle
atlas.covenantal: No part of the law passes 'till all be fulfilled'. If heaven and earth means the physical world, the whole law, sacrifices included, would still bind; so it must mean the old covenant order that ended in AD 70.
atlas.physical: A proverb for 'never' or 'as long as the world lasts'. Christ fulfils the law, and its moral force stays until the end of the world.

atlas.phrase: Heaven and earth shall pass away
atlas.covenantal: It follows 'this generation shall not pass' (24:34) and seals the temple prophecy. The old covenant world, centred on the temple, passed when Jerusalem fell in AD 70.
atlas.physical: Jesus contrasts the temporary universe with his permanent words. Many partial preterists see a turn here, or at 24:36, to the final end of the world.

atlas.phrase: easier for heaven and earth to pass, than one tittle
atlas.covenantal: 'The law and the prophets were until John' (16:16). The verse ties heaven and earth to the life of the law, so they pass together when the law's age is fulfilled.
atlas.physical: A comparison of difficulty: the universe ending is easier than God's word failing. It stresses the reliability of Scripture.

atlas.phrase: They shall perish; but thou remainest
atlas.covenantal: Hebrews was written while the old order was 'ready to vanish away' (8:13). The garment that is changed is the old covenant world; the Son remains.
atlas.physical: The writer quotes Psalm 102 to prove the Son is the eternal Creator. The created universe is changed like clothing at the end.

atlas.phrase: Yet once more I shake not the earth only
atlas.covenantal: Sinai is the first shaking (12:18-21); the second removes the Sinai order so that the unshakable kingdom, which believers 'are receiving' (12:28), remains.
atlas.physical: The final shaking is the last judgment that removes the present created order. Believers already receive the kingdom that will survive it.

atlas.phrase: the heavens and the earth ... reserved unto fire
atlas.covenantal: The 'world that then was' perished in the flood, though the planet stayed. So the present 'heavens and earth' facing fire is an order of people, judged in AD 70.
atlas.physical: As water judged the old world, fire will judge this one at the final day. The flood parallel shows a real, physical judgment.

atlas.phrase: the heavens shall pass away with a great noise
atlas.covenantal: 'Elements' (stoicheia) is Paul's word for the basic rules of the old covenant (Galatians 4:3, 9; Colossians 2:20). Those melted when the temple burned.
atlas.physical: Stoicheia commonly meant the physical elements or heavenly bodies. Early manuscripts read the earth will be 'found' (heurethēsetai), which many take as laid bare for judgment and purified.

atlas.phrase: new heavens and a new earth, wherein dwelleth righteousness
atlas.covenantal: 'According to his promise' points to Isaiah 65-66, a new covenant order. Believers in Christ already live in it.
atlas.physical: The promise is still awaited ('we look for'). It is the renewed world after the final judgment, where righteousness is at home.

atlas.phrase: the first heaven and the first earth were passed away
atlas.covenantal: The new Jerusalem is 'the bride, the Lamb's wife' (21:9-10). The new heaven and earth is the new covenant people, and the 'first' is the old covenant order.
atlas.physical: John sees the final state after the last judgment (20:11-15). The city is both a people and a place, and the old creation is renewed, with no more sea.

atlas.phrase: the whole creation groaneth and travaileth in pain together
atlas.covenantal: 'Creation' (ktisis) here may mean humanity, or Israel and the nations waiting for the revealing of God's sons. Its 'bondage of corruption' is life under sin and law, ended in Christ.
atlas.physical: The non-human creation, subjected to futility because of Adam (Genesis 3:17), will be freed with the resurrection of believers' bodies (8:23).

atlas.phrase: until the times of restitution of all things
atlas.covenantal: The restoration is what 'all the prophets' spoke (3:21-24). Peter says these days had begun (3:24), so it is the restoring of God's people in the messianic age.
atlas.physical: Christ stays in heaven until the final restoration of all creation at his return. It points to a renewed cosmos, not a covenant event alone.

worlds.label: Eden
worlds.covenantal: God makes a garden-sanctuary on a mountain, with a river and guardians. Adam serves there like a priest, since the words "work" and "keep" (Genesis 2:15) are later used of Levites in the tabernacle (Numbers 3:7-8). The covenant-creation view goes further and sees the whole of Genesis 1 as the founding of a covenant world.
worlds.traditional: God creates the whole physical universe and sets humans in a real garden within it. Eden is the first temple, but it sits inside a real cosmos that God calls very good. This is the baseline that the new creation restores and surpasses.

worlds.label: The world before the flood
worlds.covenantal: Peter says "the world that then was" perished by water. The planet survived, so what perished was a world of people and their order. This supports reading "heaven and earth" as a human, covenantal world that can end while the ground remains.
worlds.traditional: The flood was a real judgment on the physical earth and its life, though not its destruction. Peter compares it with a coming judgment by fire on the present heavens and earth. Renewal readers note the world was cleansed, not annihilated, and expect the same pattern.

worlds.label: After the flood: the covenant with Noah
worlds.covenantal: God makes a fresh start: a new command to be fruitful, a new covenant and a sign in the sky. Peter's "heavens and earth which are now" (2 Peter 3:7) can be read as this covenant order leading down through Shem and Abraham to Israel.
worlds.traditional: God promises never again to destroy the earth by a flood while it remains (Genesis 8:22). The present creation order is upheld by covenant until the final judgment. Peter's "present heavens and earth" is this cosmos.

worlds.label: Sinai: a nation founded
worlds.covenantal: Isaiah says God put his words in Israel's mouth "to plant the heavens, and lay the foundations of the earth" and to say to Zion, "You are my people". The giving of the law and the founding of the nation is a heaven-and-earth event. Moses calls heaven and earth to witness this covenant (Deuteronomy 32:1).
worlds.traditional: Isaiah speaks of the Creator of the heavens and earth who also founded Israel. Many commentators read 51:16 as joining creation and redemption, or as pointing ahead to a renewed world. The words describe God's power, not a redefinition of heaven and earth.

worlds.label: The temple: a cosmos in stone
worlds.covenantal: God built his sanctuary "like the heights, like the earth" (Psalms 78:69). The temple, with its sea, lights and inner throne-room, was Israel's heaven and earth. Josephus read it this way. When Jesus foretells its fall (Matthew 24:2), the passing of heaven and earth is close at hand.
worlds.traditional: Many traditional scholars agree the temple pictured the cosmos (Beale, Levenson). But they see it as a model pointing to the real cosmos and to God's plan to fill all creation with his presence. Its fall ends the model, while the full reality awaits the renewal of all things.

worlds.label: The exile as un-creation
worlds.covenantal: Jeremiah sees Judah formless and empty, the heavens without light. Judah's covenant world collapsed when Babylon destroyed the temple. The words are not about the planet; they describe the end of a covenant order. This becomes a pattern for AD 70.
worlds.traditional: Nearly all readers agree this is poetic language for the ruin of Judah's land. It shows the prophets can use cosmic words for historical judgment. Traditional readers simply add that the same language can also describe the final end, depending on the context.

worlds.label: The promised new heavens
worlds.covenantal: God promises new heavens and a new earth, defined at once as a Jerusalem of joy and a people of gladness (Isaiah 65:18). Death, building and planting still exist (65:20-22). So this is a new covenant world in history, not the end of physical history.
worlds.traditional: Isaiah uses familiar earthly pictures for a future renewed world. Renewal readers see the final state described in Old Testament terms. Premillennial readers often place 65:20 in the millennium. Revelation 21 takes up Isaiah's promise and makes it final, with death gone.

worlds.label: The cross and resurrection
worlds.covenantal: At Jesus' death the temple curtain, embroidered with the heavens, is torn and the earth quakes. The new creation begins on the first day of the week with the risen Christ. The old covenant is made old in principle (Hebrews 8:13), though it lingers for a generation.
worlds.traditional: All agree this is the centre: the new creation begins in Jesus' risen body (1 Corinthians 15:20). His real, physical resurrection is the pattern for the renewal of the whole creation. The final new heavens and earth are the full harvest of what began here.

worlds.label: Pentecost
worlds.covenantal: Peter says Joel's "wonders in heaven and on earth" are being fulfilled. The Spirit, the breath of new creation, is poured out. Signs in the sun and moon point to a coming day of the Lord on Jerusalem within that generation.
worlds.traditional: Pentecost begins the last days. Many say the cosmic signs in Joel are partly fulfilled at the cross and partly still future. Either way, the Spirit is the down payment of the coming new creation (Ephesians 1:13-14).

worlds.label: AD 70: the old order removed
worlds.covenantal: God shakes heaven and earth "yet once more" so that what can be shaken is removed and an unshakeable kingdom remains. The old covenant was "ready to vanish away" (Hebrews 8:13), and it did when Rome burned the temple in August AD 70 (Josephus, Jewish War 6.4.5-7). This is the passing of the first heaven and earth.
worlds.traditional: Many accept that AD 70 ended the temple system and fulfilled Jesus' words in Matthew 24:1-34. But they hold that Hebrews 12 and 2 Peter 3 reach further, to a final shaking at Christ's return. AD 70 is a real judgment and a preview of the last day.

worlds.label: The new Jerusalem
worlds.covenantal: The holy city is the bride, the wife of the Lamb (Revelation 21:9-10): the church in the new covenant. Partial preterists who hold this view see it as present now and growing, with its fullness at the resurrection. Full preterists see it as fully present since AD 70.
worlds.traditional: The new Jerusalem is the final home of God's people in a renewed creation after the resurrection. Death, mourning and pain are ended (Revelation 21:4), which has not yet happened. The city is a people, and also a place: God dwelling with his people on a new earth.

words.meaning: Heavens, sky. A plural form. It can mean the air where birds fly, the sky with sun and stars, or the dwelling of God.
words.note: The word has layers: the sky, the starry heavens and "the heaven of heavens". It is also used in poetry as a witness or a listener (Deuteronomy 32:1; Isaiah 1:2). Whether such texts mean the people of Israel, the angels or simply the whole creation called to witness is a matter of reading, not of the word itself.

words.meaning: Earth, land, country, ground. The same word covers the whole earth and one land, such as the land of Israel.
words.note: Context decides between "earth" and "land". Jeremiah 4:23-27 moves from "the earth" to "the whole land" of Judah. Covenantal readers stress this local sense. Others note that many texts clearly mean the whole earth (Genesis 1:10; Psalms 24:1).

words.meaning: Host, army, a large ordered company. Used of armies, of Israel's tribes leaving Egypt, of the stars and of angels.
words.note: Some covenant-creation writers argue that "all the host of them" in Genesis 2:1 means a mass of persons, so that the heavens and earth there are people. This is disputed. Strong's dictionary does give "a mass of persons" as a main sense, but the word is often used of the stars (Deuteronomy 4:19; Isaiah 40:26). Most Hebrew scholars read Genesis 2:1 as the full array of everything made in Genesis 1.

words.meaning: Generations, family history, "what came out of" someone. The heading word that divides Genesis into its sections.
words.note: Genesis 2:4 is the only place where toledot is used for heaven and earth rather than a person. Some covenantal readers say this shows the heavens and earth are a family of people. Most scholars say the heading means "this is what came from" the heavens and earth, that is, the story of humanity that follows. The same verse goes on to speak of God making "the earth and the heavens" as places.

words.meaning: Order, arrangement, adornment; the world, the universe, the world of humanity, or a social and religious order.
words.note: Kosmos has a wide range. In 1 Peter 3:3 it means a woman's adornment. In 2 Peter 3:6 "the world that then was" perished by water. In Galatians 6:14 the world is crucified to Paul. Covenantal readers use this range to argue that a "world" can end without the planet ending.

words.meaning: The inhabited world; often the Roman world of the first century.
words.note: Caesar's census of "all the world" (Luke 2:1) meant the Roman Empire. Agabus' famine "over all the world" (Acts 11:28) came under Claudius. So the gospel preached in all the oikoumene before the end (Matthew 24:14) can fit the first century (Colossians 1:6, 23). Futurist readers take it as the whole globe.

words.meaning: Earth, land, ground, soil, a country.
words.note: Like erets, ge can mean the whole earth or one land. "Great distress in the land" (Luke 21:23) refers to Judea. "All the tribes of the earth (land) shall mourn" (Matthew 24:30) can mean the tribes of Israel's land, echoing Zechariah 12:10-12. Revelation 21:1 uses ge for the new earth.

words.meaning: Elements; the basic parts of a series. Used of letters of the alphabet, the physical elements, the first principles of a teaching, or the heavenly bodies.
words.note: Elsewhere in the New Testament the word means the basic principles of religion: the "elements" of the world under which Israel was enslaved (Galatians 4:3, 9), the rules of Colossians 2:8, 20 and the first principles of God's word (Hebrews 5:12). Covenantal readers take 2 Peter 3:10 the same way: the old-covenant system melts. Others note that in Greek writing on the cosmos the word often meant earth, water, air and fire, or the heavenly bodies, and that the context of 2 Peter 3 is creation and the flood.

words.meaning: To pass by, pass away, come to an end, be gone.
words.note: The same verb is used for "this generation shall not pass" and "heaven and earth shall pass" (Matthew 24:34-35). Covenantal readers stress this link. Paul uses it for old things that "are passed away" in the new creation (2 Corinthians 5:17). Others say "pass away" can mean change of form, not loss of existence, as in 2 Peter 3:10, where the heavens "pass away" and the earth is "found".

words.meaning: New, fresh, of a new kind or quality.
words.note: Kainos is used of the new covenant (Hebrews 8:13), the new creation (2 Corinthians 5:17) and the new heaven and earth (Revelation 21:1). Many say it means new in quality rather than new in time, which supports renewal. Linguists warn that the difference between kainos and neos should not be pressed too hard, since the words overlap.

parallels.theme: New heavens and a new earth
parallels.note: John takes up Isaiah's promise word for word. Isaiah adds that "the former shall not be remembered"; John says the first heaven and earth "were passed away". All views agree Revelation 21 is the fulfilment of Isaiah 65-66. They differ on when and how.

Isaiah says former troubles are forgotten. John says the former things have passed away. Covenantal readers link "former things" to the old covenant and its curse. Others link them to the whole fallen order of sin, death and sorrow.

In both, the new heavens and earth are at once described as a city and its people. Isaiah's Jerusalem is created "a rejoicing"; John's comes down as a bride. This is the strongest link for reading the new creation as a people. Traditional readers answer that a people needs a place, and both are in view.
Isaiah says the voice of weeping will not be heard in the city. John adds that God himself wipes every tear and that death is no more. John's promise is fuller than Isaiah's.

parallels.theme: Death at a hundred: the puzzle
parallels.note: Isaiah says one who dies at a hundred will be counted young, and a sinner at a hundred is cursed. So death and sin still exist in Isaiah's new world, but Revelation 21:4 says "no more death". Covenantal readers say Isaiah describes the gospel age in history, with John using it as a picture of spiritual life in Christ. Premillennialists place 65:20 in a future millennium. Many amillennial and renewal readers take it as poetry: Isaiah stretches old-covenant pictures of long life as far as they go, and John gives the final reality.

Isaiah says God's people will live as long as a tree and enjoy their work. John shows the tree of life, bearing fruit every month, with leaves for the healing of the nations. Covenantal readers see the life of Christ given to the nations now. Renewal readers see Eden restored in a renewed creation.

parallels.theme: No harm on the holy mountain
parallels.note: Wolf and lamb feed together; dust is the serpent's food; nothing hurts on God's holy mountain. John says there is no more curse, and he sees the city from a great high mountain (Revelation 21:10). Some take the animals as pictures of former enemies, such as Jew and Gentile, made one (Ephesians 2:14-16). Others take them as real peace in a renewed creation, and some see both.

parallels.theme: Heaven is my throne: the temple question
parallels.note: Isaiah asks what house anyone could build for the God whose throne is heaven and whose footstool is earth. John sees no temple in the city, for God and the Lamb are its temple. Both point beyond a building made with hands. Stephen quoted Isaiah 66:1 against the temple system (Acts 7:48-50).

parallels.theme: The nations gathered to see his glory
parallels.note: Isaiah sees nations of every tongue come to see God's glory, with their gifts. John sees the nations walk by the city's light and the kings of the earth bring their glory into it. The covenantal reading sees Gentile mission now. The renewal reading sees the redeemed cultures of the world brought into the final city. Both fit the open gates.

parallels.theme: The new world remains, the rebels outside
parallels.note: Isaiah says the new heavens and earth will remain, and so will Israel's seed and name, while outside lie the bodies of the rebels. John says the overcomer inherits all things (Revelation 21:7), while outside are the dogs and liars. In both, the new world has an "outside". Covenantal readers say this shows a present age where evil still exists. Traditional readers see the final separation of the saved and the lost.

objections.q: Exodus 20:11 grounds the Sabbath in the six days when God made 'heaven and earth, the sea, and all that in them is'. Does that not prove Genesis 1 is physical?
objections.a: Most covenant readers agree. Partial preterists and many full preterists read Genesis 1 as the real creation and use covenant meaning only for later prophetic texts. The minority that reads Genesis 1 covenantally answers that the Sabbath was itself a covenant sign (Exodus 31:13-17) and that Israel's tabernacle was built in a creation pattern. Yet Exodus 20:11 lists sea and every creature, so the physical sense is hard to remove there.

objections.q: Romans 8:19-22 says the whole creation groans and will be freed from corruption. Does that not require a renewed physical world?
objections.a: The covenantal reading notes that ktisis can mean people (Mark 16:15; Colossians 1:23), and that 'earnest expectation' and 'groaning' fit people waiting for God's sons. Others in this reading accept that the physical creation is meant and say its freedom comes as God's sons are revealed, a process begun in Christ. Partial preterists keep a future bodily resurrection (8:23) and so keep a future renewal; full preterists place the 'revealing' in the first century.

objections.q: Acts 3:21 says heaven holds Christ until 'the restitution of all things'. Does that not point to a cosmic renewal at his return?
objections.a: Peter ties the restoration to what 'all the prophets' said and adds that they 'foretold of these days' (3:24). The covenantal reading sees restoration of Israel's remnant and the blessing of the nations through Abraham's seed (3:25-26), in progress since Pentecost. Partial preterists usually add that the restoration is completed at Christ's final coming; full preterists say it was completed by AD 70.

objections.q: If the dead rise with real bodies, do they not need a real renewed earth to live on?
objections.a: Partial preterists agree: they apply Matthew 24:35 and much of 2 Peter 3 to AD 70 but hold a future bodily resurrection (1 Corinthians 15:23-26; John 5:28-29) and so a renewed creation at the end. Full preterists answer that the resurrection of 1 Corinthians 15 is the raising of God's people from the death of Adam into new covenant life, fulfilled in the first century. This is the main point where the two covenant readings divide.

objections.q: Psalm 148 calls sun, moon, stars, sea monsters and hail to praise God. Does that not show 'heaven and earth' praise is physical, not symbolic?
objections.a: The covenantal reading agrees that Psalm 148 speaks of real creatures, and it does not claim that every heaven-and-earth text is a symbol. Its point is narrower: some texts, like Isaiah 49:13 or Psalm 69:34-35, tie the praise of heaven and earth to the saving of Zion. Context decides. Psalm 148 also ends with the people 'near unto him' (148:14), so creation and covenant are joined.

objections.q: Matthew 5:18 says no part of the law passes 'till heaven and earth pass'. Is that not just a way of saying 'never'?
objections.a: If it means 'never', the whole law, including temple sacrifice and food laws, would still bind today, which Hebrews 8:13 and Mark 7:19 deny. The covenantal reading says the law stood until its fulfilment ('till all be fulfilled'), and the old covenant world passed with the temple in AD 70. Others reply that Christ fulfilled the law at the cross and that its moral core lasts as long as the world.

objections.q: The church fathers and the creeds expect a coming judgment and 'the life of the world to come'. Is the covenantal reading not a modern novelty?
objections.a: On Matthew 24:35 and 2 Peter 3 the covenantal reading has older support: John Lightfoot, John Owen (on 2 Peter 3) and John Brown (on Matthew 5:18) applied the passing of heaven and earth to the Jewish order in AD 70. Partial preterists affirm the creeds fully, since they keep a future return, resurrection and judgment. Full preterists admit they differ from the creeds and appeal to Scripture as the final authority, a point other Christians find serious.

objections.q: Revelation 21:4 promises no more death, sorrow or pain. The world still has death, so how can the new heaven and earth be here now?
objections.a: Full preterists read 'death' here as the covenant death that came through sin and the law (Romans 7:9-11; 1 Corinthians 15:56), removed for those in Christ; physical death remains but has lost its sting. Partial preterists usually say Revelation 21-22 is the final state, or that it describes the church now and its full future form. Isaiah 65:20, with death at a hundred years, shows the 'new heavens' can contain physical death.

objections.q: 2 Peter 3:5-7 compares the coming fire with the flood. The flood was physical, so is the fire not physical too?
objections.a: The covenantal reading notes that the flood destroyed the 'world' of ungodly people (2 Peter 2:5), yet the planet survived. In the same way the fire judges 'ungodly men' (3:7), which was fulfilled when Jerusalem burned in AD 70. Others reply that the flood was a real event on the real earth, so the coming fire is a real, final judgment.

objections.q: Does 'elements' (stoicheia) in 2 Peter 3:10 not mean the physical building blocks of matter?
objections.a: The word can mean physical elements, letters of an alphabet, or basic rules. Paul uses it for old covenant rules (Galatians 4:3, 9; Colossians 2:8, 20; Hebrews 5:12 'first principles'). The covenantal reading takes this sense for Peter, who writes to Jewish believers in the last days of the temple. Others note Peter speaks of 'heavens' first, so heavenly bodies are a natural meaning.

objections.q: Revelation 21:1 says 'the first heaven and the first earth' passed away. Must 'first' not mean the original creation of Genesis 1?
objections.a: Most covenant readers say 'first' means the former covenant order, as Hebrews calls the old covenant the 'first' (8:7, 13; 9:1). The minority view goes further and links 'first' to Genesis 1, reading the whole creation account as covenantal. Others answer that Genesis 1 is plainly the original creation, so a renewed physical world is in view.

objections.q: Did Jesus not change subjects at Matthew 24:35-36, from 'this generation' to 'that day', the final end of the world?
objections.a: The covenantal reading says 'that day' simply means a day still future to the speaker, as 'this' marks what is near. Verse 35 confirms the whole prophecy, and the Noah comparison (24:37-41) still fits Jerusalem's sudden fall. Many partial preterists (and earlier commentators like Charles Spurgeon) see a transition here to the second coming; this is a real debate among partial preterists themselves.

nodes.q: When Jesus said 'heaven and earth shall pass away' (Matthew 24:35), was he still speaking of what 'this generation' would see?
nodes.help: Verse 34 says 'this generation shall not pass, till all these things be fulfilled'. Some readers see verse 35 as the seal on that promise; others see a turn to the end of history.

options.label: Yes, verse 35 seals the prophecy about the temple
No, it looks past AD 70 to the end of the world

nodes.q: Is 'heaven and earth' in that verse a picture of the temple and the old covenant order?
nodes.help: Josephus explained the tabernacle as a model of land, sea and heaven, and the prophets used falling stars for fallen kingdoms (Isaiah 13:10; Ezekiel 32:7).

options.label: Yes, it is covenant language for the temple world
No, it still means the physical universe

nodes.q: Did the fall of Jerusalem in AD 70 fulfil all the new heavens and new earth promises, including 2 Peter 3 and Revelation 21?
nodes.help: Full preterists say yes, including the resurrection. Partial preterists say AD 70 fulfilled Matthew 24, but a bodily resurrection and final judgment are still ahead (1 Corinthians 15:23-26).

options.label: Yes, everything was fulfilled by AD 70
No, a future resurrection and judgment remain

nodes.q: Does the covenant meaning of 'heaven and earth' reach back to Genesis 1 itself?
nodes.help: A minority of fulfilled readers say the 'first heaven and first earth' (Revelation 21:1) is the world of Genesis 1, read as the forming of a covenant people. Others keep Genesis 1 as the physical creation (Exodus 20:11).

options.label: Yes, Genesis 1 describes a covenant creation
No, Genesis 1 is the physical creation

nodes.q: How do you relate AD 70 to the final hope?
nodes.help: Some put the weight on AD 70 and keep the future hope simple: resurrection and judgment. Others say the new creation began in Christ's resurrection and will be completed in a renewed world.

options.label: AD 70 ended the old order; the future holds resurrection and judgment
The new creation has begun and will be completed physically

nodes.q: Do texts like Ecclesiastes 1:4 and Psalms 104:5, which say the earth abides for ever, shape how you read 'pass away'?
nodes.help: If the earth lasts for ever, 'pass away' may mean 'pass into a new form', like the garment changed in Psalms 102:26.

options.label: Yes, the earth will be changed, not abolished
No, those texts speak of this age only

nodes.q: In 2 Peter 3:10, is the earth 'burned up' and gone, or 'found' (laid bare) and purified?
nodes.help: Older Greek manuscripts read 'found' (heurethēsetai). Many read this as exposure for judgment and purging, like the flood (3:6). Others follow the reading 'burned up' and see the old world replaced.

options.label: Laid bare and purified, like the world after the flood
Burned up and replaced by a new creation

results.title: Physical renewal
results.text: The present universe will be purged and renewed at Christ's return, not annihilated. Romans 8:19-22 and Acts 3:21 point to creation set free. Held widely by Reformed and many evangelical teachers today.

results.title: Dissolution and replacement
results.text: The present heavens and earth will be destroyed by fire and God will make a wholly new creation (2 Peter 3:10-12; Revelation 20:11). Common in popular dispensational teaching.

results.title: Covenantal with future resurrection
results.text: Matthew 24:35 and much of 2 Peter 3 describe the end of the old covenant order in AD 70. A future bodily resurrection and final judgment remain. This is the partial preterist reading.

results.title: Full covenant-world fulfilment
results.text: All 'heaven and earth' passing texts, the resurrection and Revelation 21 were fulfilled by AD 70. The new heavens and new earth are the new covenant world believers live in now. This is the full preterist reading; Genesis 1 is still the physical creation.

results.title: Covenant creation of Genesis 1
results.text: Genesis 1 itself describes God forming a covenant people, and the 'first heaven and earth' that passed in AD 70 was that covenant world. A minority view within full preterism, contested by most because of Exodus 20:11.

results.title: Already and not yet
results.text: The new creation began with Christ's resurrection (2 Corinthians 5:17), passed a key stage when the temple fell in AD 70, and will be completed in a renewed world at his return. Many partial preterists and amillennialists hold this.

quiz.q: In Genesis 37:9-10, who does Jacob say the sun, moon and stars represent?
quiz.explain: Jacob reads the dream at once as himself, his wife and his sons. It shows heavenly lights can picture a covenant family.

quiz.q: Which Hebrew phrase from Genesis 1:2 does Jeremiah 4:23 use for Judah's ruin?
quiz.explain: Jeremiah describes the land after Babylon's attack as creation undone, using tohu wabohu.

quiz.q: According to Josephus (Antiquities 3.7.7), the tabernacle's most holy place stood for what?
quiz.explain: Josephus says the two outer parts were like land and sea, open to people, while the third was set apart for God like heaven.

quiz.q: Isaiah 13:10 speaks of stars that give no light. Which nation was the oracle about?
quiz.explain: Isaiah 13:1 names Babylon, and 13:17 names the Medes as the attackers. Babylon fell to them in 539 BC.

quiz.q: Which nation is judged when 'the heavens shall be rolled together as a scroll' in Isaiah 34:4?
quiz.explain: Isaiah 34:5-6 names Edom (Bozrah). Edom's land remained, so covenant readers see a nation's end described in cosmic terms.

quiz.q: Which text does the covenantal reading use to show the earth itself 'abideth for ever'?
quiz.explain: Ecclesiastes 1:4 says generations come and go but the earth remains. Psalms 104:5 and 78:69 say the same.

quiz.q: In Jeremiah 31:35-36, what are the sun, moon and stars used for?
options: A guarantee that Israel's place before God will last
quiz.explain: God says that only if those fixed orders fail could Israel's seed cease. The fixed sky guarantees the new covenant promise.

quiz.q: In Hebrews 12:26-28, what remains after God's final shaking?
options: A kingdom which cannot be moved
quiz.explain: Hebrews says what is shaken is removed so that the unshakable kingdom remains, and believers 'are receiving' it now.

quiz.q: How does Paul use the Greek word stoicheia ('elements') in Galatians 4:3, 9?
options: For the basic rules of the old order
For the letters of the alphabet
quiz.explain: Paul calls them 'weak and beggarly elements' tied to days and months. The covenantal reading applies this sense to 2 Peter 3:10.

quiz.q: In 2 Peter 3:6, what 'perished' in the flood, though the planet remained?
quiz.explain: Peter says the world then, overflowed with water, perished. Covenant readers stress that the planet survived and only an order of people was judged.

quiz.q: Which detail in Isaiah 65:20 makes covenant readers say the 'new heavens' are not a world without death?
options: The wolf and lamb feed together
A child shall die a hundred years old
quiz.explain: Isaiah 65:20 still mentions death and sinners. This fits a new covenant order in history better than the final state.

quiz.q: What is the main point on which partial and full preterists differ about heaven and earth?
options: Whether a future bodily resurrection and renewed creation remain
Whether Isaiah 65 is about the new covenant
quiz.explain: Both apply much of the passing language to AD 70. Partial preterists keep a future resurrection and final judgment; full preterists place them in the first century.

quiz.q: Which seventeenth-century scholar applied 'the passing away of heaven and earth' to the destruction of Jerusalem and the Jewish state?
quiz.explain: John Lightfoot (1602-1675) wrote that the Jewish state was destroyed as if the whole frame of the world were dissolved. John Owen made a similar case on 2 Peter 3.

quiz.q: Which verse is the strongest objection to reading Genesis 1 as a covenant creation?
quiz.explain: Exodus 20:11 grounds the Sabbath in the six days when God made heaven, earth, the sea and all in them. Most covenant readers keep Genesis 1 physical for this reason.
